segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏝᎩ ᎢᎾ ᏙᏓᏛᏢᏃᎮᏟ ᏄᏍᏛ Ꮕ ᎪᏪᎸ ᏛᏍᏛᏯᏛᏛᎮᏢᏂ ᎡᎾ ᏗᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᎩ ᏥᏓᏅᏕᎳᏆ ᎠᎭᏂ ᎡᎷᏭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏯᎾᏕᏠᎩ ᎠᏅᏛᎩᏍᎬ ᎢᏗᏬᏂᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎣᏏᏍ ᏍᏛᏛᎩ?
segments.translation: We’re going to talk for a while about the way it is written. I’m going to ask you all questions. The kids who are going to school, they could learn, if they hear us talking… Can you all hear OK?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: I don’t hear very well. … I’m deaf.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: It might be Michael.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Can you hear well now?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, I can hear it now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᏍᏊ ᎠᎩ,ᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩ ᎤᏠᏱ ᎾᏪᎵᏎᎰ. ᏙᎭ Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎲᏛᎩᏍᎩ ᏱᎦ ᎠᏬᏎᎰ. ᏳᏓᎭᏛ Ꮓ ᏕᏥᏍᏚᎲᏍᎪᏃ ᏳᎵᏍᎦᎮᏛᏂ. Ꮩ ᏕᏍᏛᏙ ᏳᏁᎩ ᎬᏗ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎢᎾ?
segments.translation: My wife thinks the same of me, hard of hearing. [laughs] “You can’t hear anything,” she tells me. Sometimes I just close my ears when she starts griping. [laughing] … What are y’all’s names in English and Cherokee?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.text: Carolyn Fourkiller ᎫᏫᏍᏗ Ꮕ ᏓᏩᏙ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎬᏗ
segments.translation: Carolyn Fourkiller. My Cherokee name is Gu-wi-s-d(i).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gu-wi-s-d(i), oh, OK. And you?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Me, my name is Lillie Vann.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Lillie Vann

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yes, si-na-s-d(i).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Si-na-s-d(i). Are you smart?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: No, I don’t know anything! [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you all grow up?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Well, I guess you can say Greasy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ Ꮕ ᎪᏪᎴ ᏦᎩᏁᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ Bunch ᎮᏂ Ᏺ route one route is it?
segments.translation: But we get our mail at Bunch. Route one, is it?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s Route one, yeah.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Just right there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s where you grew up?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, there in the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: In the woods.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Is that where you were born as well?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᎲᎸᏢ ᎤᏣᏘᎾ ᎠᏪᏙᎸ ᏱᎦ ᎤᎾᏭ ᎢᎦ ᎠᎩᎬᏴᎳᏥᏓ
segments.translation: I’ve never been anywhere else, just there. I’m getting old there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏣᏕᏅ ᎨᎲ ᎲᏍᏲ ᏓᎷᏆ ᏣᏕᏅ ᏱᎦ? ᎤᎾᏩ Ꭸ ᎪᎢ Ꮲ ᏣᏕᏁ?
segments.translation: Where you were born? You weren’t born in Tahlequah, were you? Or were you born there in Greasy?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎥᎲ ᎤᎾᏭ. ᏚᏁᏅᏒᏭ ᏥᏓᏂᎳᏂᏍᎬ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏍᎩ ᏄᎵᏍᏔᏂᏙᎸ
segments.translation: Yeah, it was there. They used to have babies at home. That’s how it happened.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.text: I was here in Tahlequah, ain’t it? At Hastings.
segments.translation: I was here in Tahlequah, ain’t it? At Hastings.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What year was it when you were born?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: nineteen thirty nine, ᎢᎦ ᏛᎮ ᏚᏓᎴᎾ ᏃᏭ ᏥᏨᏛᏏᏗᏒ ᎪᎢ?
segments.translation: 1939. I guess it’s all different from when you were growing up at Greasy?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎬᏛᏅᏏᏙᎲ ᎮᏂ ᎤᏩᏌ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎤᎾᏭᏅ ᏏᏭ
segments.translation: Uh-huh. I’ve been moving around, but I still come back there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏫᎯᎷᎨ Ꭱ yeah ᏙᎮ ᏣᏄᎸᎲᏍᎨ ᏣᏂᎩᏍᏗ ᏃᏭ.
segments.translation: You were having a hard time with leaving there?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about you?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: I’m the same.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The same?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Just here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK. What year was it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: nineteen seventy ok yeah ᎥᎲ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᎮᏂ Ꮓ ᏥᎦ ᏴᏛᏂ ᏕᏁᏟᏙᏗ ᎤᏂᎾᎣ Ꮓ ᏂᎾᎭ ᏙᎤᏍᏗ ᏍᏗᎮ ᏗᏍᏓᏁᏟᏙᏗ ᏥᏕᏍᏛᏛᏏᏗᏒ?
segments.translation: 1970. OK, yeah. … You could say that kids nowadays have toys to play with. What about you all? What did you all have when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏧᏂᎳᏫᏍᏗ Ꮫ ᏌᏭ ᏳᏩᎦᏗ ᏚᎾᏓᏛᏛᏅ ᏙᎬᏓᏛᏛᏅ ᏙᎤᏍᏗ ᎲᏛᏁ ᎨᎮ ᏔᏁᎶᎲᏍᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꭲ ᎤᏅᏛᏅ? ᎲᎫᏍᏗ ᏗᎫᏍᏗ ᏯᎩᎮ ᏗᏩᏁᏟᏙᏗ ᏩᎦ Ꮽ ᏣᏩᏤᎸᏒ ᏥᎦᏥᏲᎮᎸ. ᏗᏔᎷᎩᏍᎩᏅ Ꭰ ᏱᏧᎵᏍᏛᏅ ᏍᎢᎾᎾ ᎣᏂ ᎠᎬᏯᏗᏟᏅ ᏥᏌᎷᏩᏗᏒ ᏩᎦ ᎠᏩᏤᎸᏒ ᏄᏓᎴᏅ ᏯᏪᎵᏌ ᏲᎨᎵᏌ ᏙᏣᏁᎶᎲᏍᎬ ᏏᏆ ᎤᏂᏒᏍᏗ ᎤᎦᎶᎦ ᎤᏂᏢᎬ. ᎤᎾ ᏦᏥᏂᏝᎥ ᏦᎬᏒᏛ ᎣᎦᏐᎮᎸ Ꮫ ᎤᏕᎳᎰᏏ ᎣᎩᏥ
segments.translation: One time at church they asked us, “What did you do when you used to play?” they said. “Nothing! I just made-believe I was a cow!” I told them! [laughter] I made horns out of cans and wore them on the front, and I walked all bent over, acting like a cow. And if we decided to play something else, in a hog pen there used to be leaves piled up where the hogs slept. We used to lay there like the hogs did. Our mom would get onto us when she found out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎬᏂᏍᏗ Ꭸ ᎢᏥᏂᏙᎴ Ꮓ? ᎬᏂᏍᏗ Ꭸ ᎢᏥᏂᏙᎴ ᏃᏭ ᏣᏥ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏦᎮᎲ ᎡᏣᎵᏴᏅᏍᏙᏗ ᎬᏂᏍᏗ?
segments.translation: Did she use a switch on you all? Or when your mom got onto you, did she have a switch to whip you all with?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏳᏍᏗᏭ ᎨᎲ, ᏳᏍᏗᏭ ᎨᎲ ᏲᏩᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮲ ᏳᏥᏅᎩ
segments.translation: She used anything! Anything! You wouldn’t believe how far I fell [when she whipped me].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And how about you?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.text: That’s what she does to me
segments.translation: That’s what she did to me

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She did the same to you.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: The same.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎾᎾᎭ ᎭᎳᎩ ᏣᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᎨᎮ ᏃᏅ radio ᏥᏥᎩᏒ?
segments.translation: What about, how old were you when you all got a radio?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎤᏫ probably Ꮟ Ꮭ ᏱᎦᏗ Ᏺ ᏯᏩᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏎᏃ ᎠᏂ ᎬᏕᏏᏙᎯ ᏥᏄᎵᏍᏛᏅ ᎾᎯᏳ Ꮓ
segments.translation: Ooh wee! Probably, wait… I don’t remember how old I was, but when I started picking strawberries, that’s when it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You got one?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, radio.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Radio. How about the TV?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭴ ᏗᏲ ᏯᏩᏗ Ᏺ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎨᎲ Ꮭ ᎮᏂ ᏍᏊ ᎰᏩ ᏗᎬᎦᏗᏍᏗᏍᎩ ᏱᎦ ᏗᏗᏴᎸᏗᏍᎦ ᎠᏯ Ꭱ ᏙᏛ Ꮓ ᏥᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏥᎨ ᏓᎩᎪ ᏍᎩ TV ᏚᏂᏝᎲ
segments.translation: I don’t know about that one. I don’t really watch TV I was already old when I saw people having TVs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you amazed?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: For a little while. But I got used to it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You got used to it?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎢᎦᏗᏅ, ᏓᎧᏲᏐᏂ Ꮫ ᏓᏂᎧᏅ ᎤᎾᎦᏙᏍᏛ TV ᎠᏯ ᏛᏲ [ᎤᏂᏰᏥ,ᏍᎬ] Ꮭ ᎠᎭᏂ ᎮᏂ ᎤᏬᏟ ᏌᏭ
segments.translation: Some people, their eyes will dry up watching TV, but not me. [laughter] One of them is sitting here! [Carolyn]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Does she watch the wrestlers?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏗᏯᏗ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎤᎬᏙᏍᏛ. ᏍᏊ ᏂᎦ Ꭰ ᏱᎾᏮᏛᏁᎵ ᏯᎩᎶᏏ
segments.translation: I don’t know what she watches. I just glimpse at it when I go by.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Ꮎ ᏥᏨᏛᏏᏗᏒ ᏍᏈᏍᏕ Ꭸ ᏓᏓᏁᎴ ᎾᎠ ᏗᏤᏅᏒ ᎢᎾᎨ?
segments.translation: When you were growing up, were there a lot of houses near your house in the woods?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎡᎵᏴ Ꭵ ᏧᏍᏗᏭ ᏕᎬᏅᏅ ᏬᏥᎶᏍᎬ ᏲᎦᏓᏩᏛᎮᏂ
segments.translation: A ways away, yeah. We walked on the trails when we went to go visit.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: yeah, ᏥᎾᏗᎲ ᎪᎯ ᎢᎦ ᏛᎮ ᎤᏛᏁᏟᏴᏗ Ꮓ ᏙᎭ
segments.translation: Like we said, it’s changed a lot today, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: yeah, ᎪᎯ Ꮫ ᏥᎦ Ᏺ ᎤᎾ ᏗᏩᏛᏒ Ꮭ ᎠᎮ ᏱᎦᎪᎵᎦ ᏱᏌᎷ ᎠᎮ ᎢᎾᎨ
segments.translation: Yeah, it is, today. I probably wouldn’t recognize where I grew up in the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you think about it sometimes?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ, ᎠᏩᏚᎵᏍᎪ ᏩᏪᏓᏍᏗ ᎠᏎᏃ ᏲᎾ ᏕᏥᏍᎦᏱᎰ. Ꮂ ᏱᏙᎦᏥᎩ ᏯᏩᏓᎾᏫᏍᏛᏂ ᏯᎩᏰᎸᏂ ᎨᎵᎰ
segments.translation: Yeah, I want to go there sometimes, but I’m afraid of bears. I can’t outrun them, I think.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: When she’s so scared, she doesn’t realize she outruns the bear.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Ah, man, ᏂᎾᎭ ᎭᏛᏗᏍᎪ Ꭸ ᏗᏣᏛᏒ
segments.translation: Ah, man. And how about you? Do you remember when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: She was a crybaby.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was she fussy?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: We’re the same.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you two fight a lot as you all were growing up?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: When I can catch her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: This is your mother, right?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: OK. She really stayed after you?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah. Both of us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did she use a switch?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: She was carrying wood to hit us over the head with.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: One time, she was given a tricycle.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Haw!

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎡᎵ ᎦᎸᎸᏗ ᎨᎲ porch ᎠᎭᏂᏅ ᎡᎳᏗᏝ ᎨᎲ ᏝᏬᏚ ᏛᎬᏁᎲ hey ᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᏗᏓᎾᏫᏍᏗᎰ ᎣᏍᏛ ᎠᏛᏢᏍᏗᎰ ᎠᏫᏴ ᏩᎴᏫᏍᏗᎰ ᏫᏗᎶᏎ ᎤᎾ ᏢᏬᏚ ᏘᏄᏥ ᏥᏲᎮᎸ. ᏂᏥᏪᎮᎸ ᏍᎩ ᏄᎵᏍᏓᏁᎸ. ᏭᏢᏍᏛᏅᏭ ᎤᎬᏛ ᏩᎲ ᎤᎾ ᏢᏬᏚ. ᏭᎶᏛᏅ ᎾᎯᏳ Ꮓ ᏭᏁᏘᏢ
segments.translation: The porch was kind of high. And below, there were mud puddles. “Hey!” I said. She would run by me, then she’d stop. “You’re going to fall and land right in the mud!” I told her. When I said that, that’s what happened to her! She ran down and fell. Her face was right in the mud! She had had enough, then.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Haw!

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: Lillie ᎭᎳᎦ ᏂᏥᎡ ᎢᏣᏟᏅᏢ ᏂᎯ ᎭᎳᎦ ᏂᏥᎡ?
segments.translation: Lillie, how many siblings do you have? How many were you all?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: There were eight of us.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Are all of you still living?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎲᎥ, William Ross ᎯᏲᎵᎦ Ꮫ ᎨᎮ?
segments.translation: Huh-uh. Did you know William Ross?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I remember him a little.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏍᎩᏛ ᏭᏓᏂᎸᎩᎢᏴ ᎠᏯ ᎬᏟᏅᏢ ᎨᎲ ᏐᎢᎾ ᏥᏂᏏ ᏚᏙ
segments.translation: He was the oldest. And the other was named Tsi-n(i)-si [her sister].

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah, I know her.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ Jaunita Owl, ᎠᏯᏅ Ꮓ ᎤᎾ ᎾᏅ Susie Beaver, Charley ᎢᎾ Johnson ᎤᎾᏅ Ꮭ ᏰᎯ Johnson ᎡᎲ ᎣᏗᏝ ᎡᎯ ᎠᎨᏳᏥ Ꮓ Lind--Francis ᎬᏙᏲᎢ ᏚᏙᎥ ᎣᏂᏅ ᎡᎯ ᏐᏁᎵ Ꮫ ᏲᎩᏨ ᎠᏯ ᏭᏂ ᎠᏯ ᏍᎩᎾ Juanita, Charley Susie ᏅᎩ ᏛᏭ Ꮓ ᏃᏥ ᎣᏤ
segments.translation: Yeah, Juanita Owl. And me. Then, Susie Beaver. And Charley Johnson. The girl after Johnson has passed. Lind--Francis his name is, Gv-do-yo-i. He’s the last born. There were nine of us! And then me and Juanita, Charley, and Susie. There are just four of us still living.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: What about Tsi-go-ne-l(i)?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, and Tsigonel(i).

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah, there’s five.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you all still see each other? The ones still living.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Still today?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏲᏛ Ꮎ Juanita ᎤᏩᏌ Ꮭ ᏢᏢ ᎤᏂᏍᏚ ᏧᎾᏛᏅ ᏣᎾᏗᏍᎬ
segments.translation: Except for Juanita. They said she got locked up somewhere.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Are you saying Tsin(i)s(i)?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Tsin(i)s(i).

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏣᎬᏛᎦᏅᏛ Ꮎ ᎠᏙᏩ ᎤᏝᏩᏍᏓ ᏣᏅᏗᎲ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏓᎷᏫ Ꮲ
segments.translation: What I had heard was, she was staying with Adam here in Tahlequah somewhere.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏩᏥᏴᏅᎮ ᏛᏅ old timer ᎠᏎ ᏴᏓ ᎠᏂᏲᏁᎦ ᎤᏂᏁᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ Ꭰ Ꮭ ᏳᏂᏖ ᎾᏛᏁᎲ ᎤᎾᎸᏒᏂ ᏱᏓᏓᏘᎷᎦ ᎠᎾᏗᎲ. ᎤᏍᏗ ᎧᏅᏑᎸ Ꮲ ᏭᏂᏍᏚ ᏧᎾᏛᏅ. Nursing home ᎢᎡ ᎠᏥᏴᏛᏁ ᎠᎬᏱ ᎠᎮᏂ ᏓᎦᏖᎴᎬ Ꮎ ᏧᏂᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁ ᏃᎴ ᎠᏥᏅᎪᏩᏎ
segments.translation: Yeah, he came and got her. “Old timer,” I guess you’d say. That’s how the White people say it. She didn’t know what she was doing. She was mad and would attack you. They said they had her locked up in a small room. First, they put her in a nursing home, but she was fighting the workers, so they let her out of there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where all did you work?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: The longest place is…

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Bentonville Arkansas Ꮫ ᏗᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮎ ᏥᏔᎦ ᏧᏂᎯᏍᏗ
segments.translation: I worked in Bentonville, Arkansas where they killed chickens.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎤᎾᏅ ᏣᎦᏑᎪᏨ ᏃᎴ Decatur ᏍᎫ ᎤᏠᏳᏭ
segments.translation: When I quit there, then I went to Decatur, doing the same thing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The same thing.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Then, when I quit there, I went to Tyson in Stilwell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Stilwell.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You really worked, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, I liked it, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Tyson ᎮᏂ ᏧᏂᏍᏚᏅ. ᎾᎯᏳ ᎤᏛᎴᏅᎲ ᏕᏥᏲᏩᎸᎬ Arthritis ᎤᎾᏛᏅ. ᎾᎯᏳ Ꮓ ᏩᎦᏑᎵᎪᏧ ᏧᏭᏂᏍᏚᏅ ᎮᏃ ᎤᎾ
segments.translation: They closed Tyson. That’s when I started going crippled. They said it was arthritis. When they shut down Tyson, I quit working.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏙᎲ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎲᏛᏁ ᎨᎮ ᏥᏔᎪ ᏥᏕᏣᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎲ?
segments.translation: What were you doing, working at the chicken plant?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: I was cleaning and processing (pulling from the rear end) chickens. They would go by on the conveyor.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were fixing them?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: I was using snips.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎾᏅ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏗᏝ ᎠᏂᏙᎾᎥ Ꮎ ᏧᎵᎦᏌ ᏗᏂᎾᏒᏁᏍᎩ
segments.translation: And then after me, others were standing there to pull the guts out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess you would say there were chickens everywhere there.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: A lot of them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And how about you? Where all did you work?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Wait…

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: She lived over in Arkansas at first.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.text: little rock, little rock UAMS ᎤᏔᏂ ᎠᏓᏁᎵ yeah. Nurse nurses aid
segments.translation: Little Rock. In Little Rock, I worked at the UAMS building. Nurse’s aid.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, OK.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: About 20 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: 20 years.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: And at Tyson for a little bit.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah, Tyson for a bit.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: You were inspecting the meat.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah, frozen meat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: inspector Ꭾ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏙᏍ well ah be. ᏴᏛᏂ ᎤᏂᎸᏩᎦᏓ ᏥᎨᎰ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎤᎾᏛᏗ. ᏘᏃᎩᏍᏗᏍ Ꭸ ᏂᎯ?
segments.translation: Oh, inspector, eh? Well, I’ll be. You could say people liked to come and do something. Do you play music?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you play guitar (pluck/pinch/scratch)?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Huh-uh. I can scratch somebody.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you go where ticks are.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And how about you?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don’t have no hobby, huh?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.text: nope, no hobby Ꮭ just taking care of [her].
segments.translation: Nope, no hobby. Just taking care of [her].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you all go to church?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: I do. Rock Fence.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Rock Fence nvyi disoyv.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: nvya disosdv.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you sing in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏙᏥᏃᎩᏍᎪ Ꮫ ᏗᏣᎳᎩ ᏗᎾᎴᏂᏍᎩ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎣᎩᎦᏘ judge fourkiller ᏚᏙ ᎯᏲᎵᎩᏍ?
segments.translation: We sing. But our pastor, Judge Fourkiller, do you know him?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꮭ ᎩᎶ ᏄᏓᎴ ᏗᎴᏂᏍᎩ ᏱᎨᎮᏍᏗ ᎠᏯᏭ ᎠᏭᏏ ᏧᏛᏅ. ᎣᎩᏑᎵᎪᏧ ᏳᏓᎭ ᏩᎩᎵᏰᏗᎰ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏙ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏙᏗᎧᏂᎩᏍᎬ
segments.translation: He said nobody was going to lead songs but him. We just all quit. Sometimes I just moan around, ’cause I don’t know what he’s singing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎡᎵᏭ Ꭸ ᏱᏃᎩ ᏌᏭ? ᏌᏭ ᎤᎾᏓᏝᎬᏭ ᏱᎦ
segments.translation: Could you sing one? One verse?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: One?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, one verse.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: The Lord’s Son.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Alright.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎤᏁᎳᏅ ᎢᏳᏪᏥ ᎢᎦᎫᏴᎮᏱ ᏦᏒ ᎾᏊ ᏫᏳᎶᏎ ᎢᎦᎫᏴᎮᏱ ᎠᏎᏃᏱ ᎤᏁᏨᏱ ᎢᏳᏃ ᏚᎴᏅ ᏔᎵᏁ Ꮫ ᏥᎷᏥᏟ ᎤᏛᏁ ᏳᏁᏤᎠ
segments.translation: “The Lord’s Son paid for our sins. And went to Heaven, he paid for us. But He spoke, when he rose up. He said he will come again.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Amen, amen.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That is good.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: I went into the second verse.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s a beautiful song.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It sounds like somebody’s preaching when they sing that song.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏨᏌ ᏱᏃᎩ ᏱᏣᏓᏛᏓᏍᏗ Bible ᎢᎦᏓ ᏙᏗᎪᏪᎵ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏂᎦᏪ
segments.translation: If you sing and listen to yourself, some of what the Bible says is in there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: yeah, ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᏧᎾᏁᏟᏗ ᎤᎾᏓᏢᎬ ᏕᏥᎦᏘ Kenwood ᏗᏝ Steely ᏧᏙᎩᏓ
segments.translation: I’m a pastor of Christians in Kenwood. Steely is what it’s called.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎡᏧᎳ ᎮᏂ ᏓᏂᏃᎩᏍᎪ ᏲᏁᎦ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ Ꮕ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎢᎦᎵᎡᎵᎪ ᎠᏯ
segments.translation: They sing in both Cherokee and English. I really appreciate it.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎠᏯ Ꮫ ᏲᏁᎩ ᎨᎲ Ꮭ ᎰᏩ ᏱᏗᏥᎦᏔ
segments.translation: I don’t really know them in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎩᎶ ᎡᏲ ᏱᏗᎧᏃᎩ ᏴᏩᏘ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏕᎧᏃᎩᏍᎬ Ᏺ ᏱᏥᏍᏕᎵ
segments.translation: If someone else is singing I know what they’re singing and I help them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᎮᏂ Ꮭ Judge Fourkiller ᏳᏍᏗ ᏱᎦ ᎠᏯ. ᏱᏓᎩᏃᎩᏏ ᎮᏂ ᏱᏛᎾᏂᎩ
segments.translation: I’m not like Judge Fourkiller. If I sing, they’ll probably go home.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: You don’t just go cry?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many children do you have?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: well ᏑᏓᎵ Ꮫ ᏂᎦᏓ ᎨᎲ ᏂᎦᏗ Ꮕ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏁᎯ
segments.translation: Well, there’s six of them altogether. And all six are still alive.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do they all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏲᏁᎦᎭ Ꮫ ᏓᏅᏟᏃᎮᏍᎪ ᏙᎤᏍᏗ ᎭᏗ grandma ᏯᏅᏗᏅ ᏨᎩᎵᏌ? ᏗᏩᏘ ᏥᏣᎳᎩ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏯ ᎦᏥᏲᎮᎰ
segments.translation: They just all speak in English. My grandkids will say, “What’re you saying, Grandma?” – “I don’t know. I’m Cherokee,” I tell them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎠᏎᎾ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᎠᏲᏟ ᏳᏕᏂ ᏝᏍᎫ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏱᎦᏬᏂ ᏲᏁᎦᎭ ᎤᎾᏝᏃᎮᏙ ᎠᏛᏍᎪ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ
segments.translation: But nowadays, when a child is born, they talk to it in English. Today.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, today.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎠᎬᏱᏅ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ Ꮕ ᎠᏯ Ꮕ ᏗᏩᏛᏒ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎠᎫᏏ Ꮕ school ᎢᎾ ᎠᏩᎴᏅ Ꮓ ᎤᎾ ᎠᏩᏕᎳᏆᎥ ᏍᏗ ᏲᏁᎦ ᎠᎩᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ. ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎫᏌ ᏭᏅ ᏱᎦ ᏥᏬᏂᏍᎦ ᏥᎨᏒ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎡᎵᏌ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎧᎵ ᎮᏂ ᎠᎫᏌ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎡᏚᏓ Ꮎ ᏍᎫ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎡᏥᎾ. ᎡᏙᏓ ᎡᏲ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎧᎵ Joe Vann.
segments.translation: At first, when I was growing up it was Cherokee and Creek. But then, when I started going to school, I learned to speak English. Before, I was just speaking Cherokee and Creek. My grandmother and grandfather were full-blooded Creek. And my mother. My dad was a full-blood Cherokee, Joe Vann.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Roy Vann?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Josiah Vann.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your dad isn’t alive now?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: No, it’s been a while.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s been a while.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.text: ᏏᏍ ᎤᎪᏗ ᎫᏌ ᎯᏬᏂ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ?
segments.translation: Can you still speak a lot of Creek today?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Huh?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.text: ᏏᏍ ᎤᎪᏗ ᎫᏌ ᎯᏬᏂ ᎯᏬᏂᏍᎪ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ?
segments.translation: Can you still speak a lot of Creek today?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: yeah, ᏱᏥᏬᏂ ᎢᏛ ᎪᎵᎪ Ꮕ ᏍᏊ Ᏺ ᏂᎦᏓ ᎾᏂᏪᏍᎬ ᎫᏍᏓ. ᎠᏎᎾ ᏱᎾᎦᎵᏍᏗ ᏱᏥᏬᏂᎯ ᎮᏂ Ᏺ ᏍᏗ
segments.translation: Yeah, I can speak and I understand everything they say. But, when I have to, I speak it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Can you sing any Creek songs that they sing?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏝᏲ ᏱᎨᎵ Ᏺ ᏍᎩᎾ. ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏍᎫ ᎤᏂᏃᎩᏍᏓ Ꮭ ᏱᎦᏥᏃᎩ. ᏲᏁᎦ Ꮽ ᎬᏗ
segments.translation: I don’t think so. I can’t sing the Cherokee songs either. Just in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏢᎲ Ᏺ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎦᎵᏍᏙᏗ ᏱᎦᎯᏃᎩ? Lillie ᏗᎨᏣᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏙᎤᏍᏗ ᏚᎾᏙᎡ? ᏣᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: You probably can’t sing anything! [laughs] Lillie, your parents, what were their names? Your late father.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Frank Ross – Dvnowelan(i).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dvnowelan(i)? Well, I’ll be!

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎡᏥ Ꮎ ᏩᎵ Polly Vann ᏚᏙᎡ ᎠᏎ ᎣᏂᏴ ᏧᏂᏃᎮᏢ ᎩᎶ ᎤᏁᏟᏴᏒ Ꮟ ᏗᏩᏕᎳᎰᏒ ᎮᏂ ᎡᏚᏣ ᏫᎳ ᏚᏙᎥ. ᎡᏥ ᎤᏙ Ꮎ check ᏯᏥᏃᎮᎵ ᏧᏂᎾᏝ ᎠᏂ ᏓᏫᏒ ᏗᏂᎶᎩᏍᎦ bill Scott ᏍᎩ ᏂᎦᏪᏍᎬ ᎠᏥᏯᏂᎲ ᎠᏥᏅᏁᎲ ᏢᏢᏴᏃ Vann ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏅᏘ ᏍᎩ ᏄᏛᏁᎸ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏄᎵᏍᏓᏂᏙᎸ ᏭᏓᏁᏟᏴᏒ
segments.translation: My mom, her name was Wal(i) – Polly Vann. Later on, they said that somebody had changed it, but I remember my uncle; his name was Wil(i). He was my mom’s brother. When they brought his check from people that owned the strawberry patch – they had people working for them – they called him Bill Scott. There wasn’t a Vann anywhere! I don’t know what happened that made it change.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎠᏂ scott ᎮᏂ ᏲᏙ ᏧᏛᎴᏅᎲ Ᏺ ᏙᎭ
segments.translation: But it was Scott at the beginning, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, Bill Scott.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: They changed it for him.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: That’s what it said when they gave him a check.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: So he just kept that name?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᎭᏅᏛᏗᏍᎪ Ꭸ Ꮎ ᎯᎨᏳᏣ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏙᎠᎾᏛᏁ ᎨᎮ ᎢᏣᎵᏍᏕᏠᏗ ᏚᏂᏫᏒᏁ Ꭸ ᏙᎨ
segments.translation: Do you remember, when you were a girl, what they did to make a living? Did they have a garden? Or?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ, ᏚᏂᏫᏒᏅ ᏥᎨᎲ. ᎡᏙᏓ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᏫᏒᏍᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏎᎷ ᏧᏫᏒ ᎠᏂ Ꮕ ᏓᏂᎶᎩᏍᎬ ᎠᏂᏰᎲᏍᏗᎲᏂ ᏕᎩᏥᎾᏝᎥ ᏗᏝ ᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᏯ ᎣᏥᏅ ᏦᎩᎾᏛᏂᏓ Ꮕ ᎠᏯ Ꮎ Juanita ᏙᎩᏂᎦᏘᏗᏍᏛ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ Ꮒ ᎤᏛᏅ ᏩᎦ ᎤᏂᎷᏨ ᎠᏂ star ᏧᎾᏤᎵ ᎤᏂᎪᏗ. ᎢᎾᎨ Ꮽ ᎠᏁᏙ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏩᎦ ᎾᎯᏳ. Ꮒ ᏫᏗᏍᏚ ᎠᏭ ᏩᎦ Ꭱ ᎠᎩᎾ ᏓᏅᏘᏁ ᏱᏕᏗᏁᎩᏎ ᎤᏅᏓ ᎤᏛᏅ. ᎰᏩᏅ ᎣᎨᎵᏒ ᎣᎩᏍᏚᎢᏒ ᎩᎶᏫᏛ ᏱᎪᎯᏓ ᎤᎾᎵᏝᎥᏍᏛᏅ Ꮎ ᏩᎦ ᎥᏂᏴᏢ ᎣᎩᏍᏚᎢᏌ ᎾᏅ ᏎᎷ ᎤᎾᏚᎵᎮ. Ꭴ ᎤᏛᏅ ᏃᎴ Ꮎ ᏎᎷ ᎠᎾᏓᏲᏍᏓᏁᎠ. ᏃᎴ ᏙᏥᎨᎯᏙᎸ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᎷᏣ Ꮓ ᎭᎴ ᏂᏙᎩᎸ. ᏱᎬᏕᎵᎦᏅ ᎦᎶᎪᏓ ᏫᏚᏴᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꮎ ᎢᏗᎶᎦᎦ Ꮎ ᏚᎾᎳᏍᎬᎠ ᎤᏛᏅ ᏚᎾᎳᏍᎬ Ꮽ ᏱᎬᎾᏕᎾ ᎣᎩᎶᎦᏅ ᎣᏨᏍᎬᏢᏍᎬ ᏩᎦ ᏎᎷ ᏥᎨᏛ
segments.translation: Yeah, they had gardens. My dad was a planter. He planted corn and strawberries. The workers plowed for the plants to grow. We were all sitting there, us older ones. Like, Juanita. They left their kids for us to babysit. “Look!” she said. The cows came, a whole lot of them. They belonged to the Starrs. The cows roamed in the woods back then. She said, “Look! Let’s open it! The cows are bringing calves, let’s get milk from them.” We believed them, so we opened it. Those cows just came running in, fast, when we opened it. They were wanting the corn! [laughter] She said, “Ooh! They’re ruining the corn!” Then we had to chase them off. Then when Dad got home, we almost got killed. He turned around and picked up the hoes. “Let’s plow up the cow tracks!” So, we plowed just where the cows’ tracks were hiding. And the corn was standing up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏣᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎾᎨ Ꮎ ᏐᏫᎳ ᏗᎬᏗᏍᎦ ᎨᎲ ᏳᏩᏓᎷᎦᏂ?
segments.translation: Your late father, did he use horses to plow with?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏐᏫᎵ ᏗᎬᏗᏍᎦ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏗᎦᏓᎷᎩᏍᎦ ᏧᎾᏓᎴᏅᏓ ᏴᏩ ᎾᎠ ᎡᎵᏴ ᏙᏗᏂᏁᎸ ᎠᏂᎷᎪ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏗᎨᏥᏓᎷᎦᏁᏗ ᎤᎾ ᏫᏗᎦᏓᎷᎩᏍᎪ ᏥᎨᎲ. ᏗᏗᏍᏗᎾ ᏗᎪᏢᏍᎩ ᏨᎨᎲ ᎣᏥᏟᏏᏍᎩ Ꮕ ᎠᏯ Ꮎ rough Ꭲ ᏳᏍᏗ Ꮭ ᏱᏚᏩᏯ ᎤᎾᏓᏕᏒᏗ Ꮫ ᏫᏗᎦᏁᏍᎪ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏓ Ꮕ ᎦᎾᎸᏗᏍᎬ Ꮎ ᎤᎾᏓᏕᏒᏗ Ꮎ ᎠᏂᏗᏝ ᎦᏙᎦ ᎤᏂᏗ ᎠᎭᏂᎾ ᏗᏝ ᎠᏗᏍᏓᏂ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏗᏝ ᏫᎫᏓᎸ ᎣᏥᎾᏌᎾᏫᏗᎲ ᎤᏩᏅᏕᏍᎬ ᏫᏙᏣᏓᏕᎲ. ᏳᏓᎭ ᏫᏥᏛᏅᎬ ᏱᏓᎩᏲᏢ ᏍᏓᏯ Ꮫ ᏙᎩᎾᏝᎥ ᏙᎬᏛᏏ Ꭴ
segments.translation: Yeah, he used horses to plow. And then people that lived nearby would come and ask him to plow for them. He went and plowed for them. He used to make railroad ties, and we had to gather them up. He would have them in some kind of rough spot. He would go get a rope. On the rope, he would have a stick, so one can pull it from one side and another from the other side. He would have the railroad tie tied with the rope, and we would drag it. We would take them where they were piled up. Sometimes I would fall and the rope would turn loose. They had us working hard, growing up. Ooh!

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: Ꮎ Ꭸ ᏍᎫ ᏱᎦ ᎢᎾᎨ ᎢᏥᏴᎸᏍᎨ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎾᎯᏳ?
segments.translation: Did you all also search for wild foods in the woods back then?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Onion and poke.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Onion, there used to be a lot of different things growing, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: And how about that the green stuff they call it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, the green stuff.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎪᎢ ᎤᏗᏝᎦ ᏯᏍᏚᏝ ᎤᏖᏓ ᎠᎩᏍᏓ ᏔᏩᎵ ᎢᎾ
segments.translation: If you pour hot grease on it, it’s real good to eat. And then, tawal(i)!

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏙᎲ ᎤᏍᏗ ᏍᎩᎾ? Ꭵ ᏙᎩ ᎤᏍᏗ ᏣᏗ?
segments.translation: What is that? What is it you said?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏔᏩᎵ Ꭰ ᎡᎯ ᏛᏲ Ꮲ ᎤᎾ ᏗᏝ Ꮎ rough Ꭲ ᎨᎲ Ꮎ ᏔᏩᎵ ᏚᏙ ᏗᎦᏅᎯᏗ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏧᎦᎶᎩ Ᏼ ᏂᏕᎦᏅ Ꭰ ᏳᎵᏍᏛᏅ ᏩᏥᎸᏍᎪᏂ ᏍᎫ ᎤᏬᏚ ᏝᏲ ᏯᎩᎸᏫᎦᏛᏁ Ᏺ ᎠᏯ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏔᏩᎵ ᎨᎲ Ꮎ ᎠᏂᏐ Ᏺ ᎤᏂᎸᏫᎦᏔᏁ ᎾᏅ ᎪᏧᏂ ᏣᏃᏎᎰ ᎠᎹᏳᏟᏗ ᎢᎦᏓ ᏍᎫ ᎠᏂᎩᏍᎪ Ꮭ ᏯᎩᎪ Ᏺ ᎠᏯ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᏟᏅ ᎠᎹᏯ ᎤᏚ
segments.translation: Tawal(i). It still grows over here. It’s got long leaves and it’s kinda rough. It’s called tawal(i). It blooms really pretty flowers. I didn’t like it, but the others did. And then that kotsun(a) they call it. It grows by the water. Some people eat that, but I don’t like that either. And watercress.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s real good.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏳᏍᏗ ᏛᎮ ᎨᎲ ᎣᏥᎩᏍᎨ ᎪᎵ ᎫᏂᏍᎩ ᏧᏛ ᎤᏩᏱᏢ Ꮲ ᏩᎦ ᏩᏩᏤᎸᎣ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏥᏂᎪ ᎬᏗ ᎦᏕᏍᎬ ᎤᏖᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᎩᏍᏓ Ꭰ ᏫᏂᎬᏛᏁᎰ
segments.translation: We ate just anything. There was always huckleberries there. I would pretend to be a cow eating the huckleberry bush. Using my tongue, I was taking berries off. It was good to eat. I was going like this [gestures].

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You were sticking your neck out?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏩᎦ ᏃᏭ ᏩᏩᏤᎸᏒ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎣᏤᏙᎲ ᎣᏥᎩᏍᎬ ᏒᎵᏅ ᎧᏂᎩ ᎧᏩᏯ ᏕᎲ ᎬᏄᎦᏟᏅ
segments.translation: Yeah, I was acting like a cow while we were there, we were just eating. There were no persimmons. Huckleberries and blackberries.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: “Kanig(a).” What is that?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Blackberries – kanugatl(i), ain’t it?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏣᎳᎩ ᏭᎾ ᏱᎦ ᏄᏓᎴ ᏠᏏᏅᏗ Ꮎ ᎠᏃᎮᎰ ᎤᏠᏳᏭ ᏏᏭ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎡᎳᏗᏭ ᎠᏛᏍᎦ Ꭰ ᏱᏗᎦᏓᏍᏗᏍᎦ ᏠᏏᏅᏗ ᎾᏅ ᎧᏄᎦᏟ Ᏺ ᎢᎾ ᏱᎦᏓ Ꭴ ᏧᏣᏲᏍᏗ ᏍᎫ ᏱᎦ ᎠᏩᏅᏘ. ᎤᏂᏍᎫᏱ ᏱᏕᎰ ᏙᎸᏥ ᏣᏅᏛᏛᏍᎪ ᏍᎫ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏦᏥᎩᏍᎪ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᏂᏖᏗ ᏗᎩᏍᏗ ᏍᎩᎾ. ᎮᏍᏕᎡ ᏯᏁᎯ Ꮓ. ᎯᎸᏍᏄᏒᏭᏃ
segments.translation: Only in Cherokee, they are different. Tlosinvd(i), they call it. It looks the same as blackberry. It just grows short, but blackberries grow tall. And ooh! They’ve got thorns. That’s all I know. Oh, and there’s unisguy(i) – they grow on an oak tree. That’s what we ate, too. Those were good to eat. They’re not around anymore. A few days ago…

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: You ate them up, I guess!

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎲᎸᏍᏄᏒᏭ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏥᏃᎮᏍᎬ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꭱ ᎤᏂᏍᎫᏱ ᏦᏥᎩᏍᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎭᏢ ᏳᏘ ᎠᎵᏒᎲᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᎢᎾᎨ ᎡᎯ ᏍᎫ ᎠᏓᏢᏗ
segments.translation: I was talking about it a few days ago. “We used to eat unisguy(i), but they’re not around anymore,” I told them. It’s not hanging anywhere! The wild foods are disappearing. They’re going away!

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: How about that uyahvti … uyahvti.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Uyahvti, yeah…

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Do you like that?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Do you like uyahvti?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Huh-uh. I’ve never tried it.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎠᎩᎸᏫᎦᏓ Ᏺ ᎠᎩᏍᏗ Ꮎ vine ᏥᏄᏍᏙ ᎤᎵᏙᎸ ᎠᎩᎸᏩᎦᏗ ᎡᏲ ᎠᎩᏍᏗ Ꮭ ᏯᎩᎸᏫᎦᏓ ᏙᏲ ᎤᎦᎾᏍᏗ
segments.translation: I like to eat it. The vine that’s on there. I like that and it is really sweet.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What is that in English?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I don’t know!

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏍᎨ ᏓᏩᏝᎪ ᏑᏓᎴᎦ ᎨᎲ ᏲᏁᎩ ᎬᏗ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏣᏗ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎢᎦᏓ Ᏺ ᎠᏩᏅᏘ
segments.translation: I can’t remember some of those in English. I know some of them.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎡᏙᏓ ᎡᏲ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᎸᏫᎦᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ Ᏺ Ꮎ ᎤᏯᎲᏗ. ᎠᏛᏲ Nicut lee creek ᏣᎾᏗᎰ ᎠᎹᏯ ᏳᏟᏗ ᎤᎾ Ꮴ ᏍᎩᎾ
segments.translation: My dad used to like to eat uyahvt(i). It grows over at Nicut by the water at Lee Creek.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it still growing today, you think?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Huh?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you think it’s there now?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᎡᎯ ᏛᏏ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎲᏙ ᎣᏍᏗ ᏱᎦ
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s still there. But, it’s not really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Ꮭ ᎣᏍᏗ ᏱᎦ. ᏙᏅ ᎡᏘᏴ ᏥᎨ ᏍᏈᏍᏓ ᏤᎾᎥ ᎢᎾᎨ ᎬᏩᏛᏗ ᎠᏎᎾ ᏃᏝ ᏚᏂᎶᎨᏗ ᎮᏂ ᎢᎦᏗ ᎦᏙ ᏧᏂᏩᏍᎩ
segments.translation: It’s not good. … Really, a long time ago, there were a lot of things to find growing in the woods. But not now. They’re plowing it up, the people who are buying the land.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏙᏛ Ᏺ ᏍᎩ ᏄᏍᏗ Ꮓ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ. ᏂᎬ ᎮᏂ ᏚᏂᎶᎩ ᏗᏓᏁᎸ ᎮᏂ ᎾᎠ ᏂᎬ ᎮᏂ ᏕᎦᎶᎩ ᏦᏥᏁᎵ
segments.translation: That’s true. That’s how it is today. They’re plowing all over. Even by the house, they’re plowing all over where we live.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏐᎢᎾ ᎨᎲ Ꮭ ᏳᎦᏲᏗ ᏝᎧ? ᎤᎾ ᏧᏮᏙᎲ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎪᎯᎦ. ᎤᎾ ᏫᏛᎨᏙᎵ ᏲᎵᏌ
segments.translation: Another thing, you can’t go into the land. Because the owners won’t let you.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᎤᏂᏅᏍᏙ no trespassing ᏛᏰᏣᏂᏢᏂ ᏯᏅᏗ. ᎤᎾ Ꮕ Ꮲ
segments.translation: Yeah, they’ve got those “No Trespassing” signs. “They’re going to sue you!” they’ll say.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: That’s what they’ll do now.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎤᏕᎸᏛ ᏳᏩᎩᎷᏥ ᏳᎦᏛᎾᏏᏅᏍᏗ ᏱᏫᏥᏄᏴ ᏥᎦᏥᏲᎮᎲ ᏯᏩᏚᎵ ᎫᏍᏗ inside
segments.translation: “I would hide and crawl under, if I want something inside,” I told them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They’ll shoot you.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏍᎫ Ꮫ ᏱᎦ Ꮓ no trespassing
segments.translation: That’s it. No trespassing.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎠᏎᎾ ᎯᎾ ᎣᏂ ᏧᎾᏛᏒ ᏣᏁᎭ ᏝᏅ ᏍᎩ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎠᏂᎩᏍᎩ ᏱᎦ
segments.translation: The generation today, they don’t eat things like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: They hate it.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: They don’t recognize it.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: We ate hog guts back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we did, too.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: And the head.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: She’s got some.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: She’s got two in the freezer.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: There’s two hog heads in there.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏔᎵ ᏙᏗᎩᏝ ᏏᏆ ᏧᏍᎦ freezer Ꭲ ᏥᏍᎷᏴᏛ ᏛᎩᏂᏍᏛᏂ ᎦᏗᎲ Ꮂ ᏍᎩᎦᏙᏍᏙᏗ ᏥᎩᏍᎨᏍᏗ ᎦᏥᏲᎮᎲ
segments.translation: I’ve got two in the freezer, hog heads. When I slice it up, I’m going to cook it. “I guess you’re all just gonna watch me while I eat it,” I told them.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: And some cornbread.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you like the hog ears?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎥᎲ yeah, ᎤᏂᏖᏗ ᏍᎫ ᏗᎩᏍᏓ ᏍᎩᎾ. ᎾᏅ ᏧᏬᏰᏂ
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah. Those are really good to eat. And then the hands.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The hands. How about the feet?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, the feet.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: I’ve seen them preparing that.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏯᎪᎲᏍᏛᏂ ᎮᏂ ᎤᎳᏍᏕ ᏏᏆ ᏩᏂᎨ ᏱᏂᎦᎵᏍᏗ Ꮎ ᏍᏓᏯ ᎤᏑᎬᏢ ᏱᏕᎪᎰ ᏃᏭᏅ ᏧᏓᏅᎬᎸᏗ ᎭᏫᎾ ᏗᏝ ᏗᏍᏗᎩᏍᏓ. ᏌᎵᎫᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏍᎫ ᏦᏥᏰᏍᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: When you burn them, the feet, they’ll get tender. And then you can knock off the hooves. Then it’s clean on the inside. You can eat them. We used to eat snapping turtles.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we did, too.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: And frog legs.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Y’all were really eating well back then.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏥᎦᏥ Ᏺ ᎮᎲ ᏍᎩᏛ ᏳᏍᏗ Ꮟ ᏥᏥᏙᎩ ᏥᎦᏥᏲᎮᎲ. ᎾᏅ ᎤᏪᏘ ᏛᎮ date ᎢᎾ Ꮭ ᎩᎶ ᏱᎬᏩᏗ Ᏼ ᎦᏝᏛᏅ ᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏥᎦᏥᏲᎮᎸ
segments.translation: I tell them, “That’s why I’m still standing here!” And then, “[Check] The date, you don’t know how long ago it was canned,” I said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, no.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: I still say that now.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᎠᎹᏝᏗᏍ ᎢᏦᏢᏎ Ꮭ Ꭸ ᎬᏅᎪᎬ ᏫᏥᏁᎩᏍᎨ ᎠᎹ ᏥᏕᏣᏍᏗᎬ?
segments.translation: When you all were little, did you all have a well? Or did you get water from a spring?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏍᎩ ᏍᎫ ᏨᎬᏛᏛᎲᏍᎬ ᎯᏭ last week ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮲ ᎤᎾ ᏦᏤᎲ ᎤᎾ ᏳᏬᎩᎦᏐᏏ ᎢᎾᎨ. ᎢᎾᎨ ᏬᏥᎦᏐᏍᎪ Ꭰ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᏕᏯᏛᏛ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏄᏍᏛ ᎤᎾ ᏲᎩᎶᏐᏂ ᏃᎴ ᎤᎾ ᏩᎬᏅᏅ ᏐᎢᎾ ᏙᏩᎴᎳ ᏧᏟᏓᏍᏗ ᏥᏂᎦᏅᎾ ᎠᏫᏴ ᎤᏬᏛ ᏥᏄᏍᏛ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏅᏘ ᏄᏍᏛ ᏃᏭ Ꮭ ᎠᏪᏙᎸ ᏱᎦ. ᎯᎢ ᏄᎵᏍᏓᏂᏢ Ꮎ ᎦᏓ ᎤᎾ ᏧᎦᏒᏛ ᏅᏱ ᎤᏔᏂ. ᎤᎾᏅ ᎯᎢ ᏄᏍᏛ ᏅᏱ ᎤᎾ ᏥᏓᏔᎴᏒ. ᎤᎾ ᏥᏓᎧᎵᏥᎯᎲ ᎠᎹ ᎤᎾ ᏬᏥᏃ ᏥᎨᎲ. Ꮎ gallon Ꮧ ᏕᎦᏟᏓ ᎤᏏᏕᏂ ᏕᎦᏇᏗᎲ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎪᎩ ᏱᎦ ᏍᏓᏯ ᎯᏛ ᏂᏕᏉ ᏍᎩᎾᎾ ᏙᏥᏟᏍᏗᎲ ᏙᏥᏫᏗᎲ. ᏬᏥᎦᏐᏍᎬ ᎢᎾᎨ. ᎪᎯᏗᏅ ᎣᎩᎦᏘᏗᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎣᏥᎫᎩᏍᎬ ᏙᏥᎬᎵᎢᎲ ᏃᎴ ᏙᏥᏍᏚᏟᏍᎬ Ꮎ wet ᏂᏙᏨᏁᎲ ᏕᎦᏝᏗ ᎩᎵᏅ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏲᎩᏍᏋᏗ ᎩᎳ ᏗᎣᏣᏂᎩᏍᎬ ᎢᎾᎨ ᎣᏨᏨᏏᏰᏍᎬ ᎠᎹ ᎣᎩᏲ. ᎪᎯᏅ ᏥᎦ ᏢᏍᎫ ᎠᏭᏭ ᎤᏒᏛ ᏳᎬᏂᏁᎦ ᎠᎹ ᏯᏂᎾᎵ. ᎠᎭᏂ ᎮᏂ ᎤᏬᏟ ᏌᏭ ᎨᎲ
segments.translation: That’s what they were asking me, just about a week ago. Where we lived, we would go downhill into the woods. There, there was an embankment of water, and we would go past it. Then there was a wagon trail there. It was pretty there, but I don’t know what it’s like now, I haven’t been there. Where this [gestures] happened, there was a big rock sticking out of the ground. The rock was like this [gestures], and there were big holes. And that’s where the water was coming in. We used to sit there. My dad used to wrap gallon jugs in a thick cloth for a while, real tight. They were this [gestures] big. That’s what we put the water in and would take with us. We would go downhill into the woods. We had to wait for a while, while we drew the water and filled the jugs. Then we’d splash water on them to get them wet. Then we’d leave when we were done. We were walking into the woods to get water. And today, they won’t even go get water behind the house, ’cause they’re so lazy. There’s one sitting right here!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Is that true, Soldier?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were really hiding it, ain’t it? They talk about you.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: yeah, ᏙᎮᏲ ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᏂᎨᎲᏂ ᏱᎦ ᎠᎪᏂ ᏯᏂᎾ
segments.translation: Yeah, if it wasn’t for me, they would be starving.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏂᎾᎭ ᎠᎬᏱ ᏥᏕᏣᏕᎳᏆᎥ ᏲᏁᎩ Ꭸ ᎯᏬᏂᏍᎩ ᎨᎮ?
segments.translation: What about you? When you first went to school, did you speak English?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Yeah, I did speak.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah, Greasy Headstart.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you pass the grade?

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᎡᏧᎵᏭ ᏛᎧ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏙᎭ ᎦᏬᏂᏓ ᏲᏁᎦ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ Ꮕ
segments.translation: It was both of them back then, ain’t it? Speaking English and Cherokee.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And how about you? Where did you say you went to school?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏅᏯ ᏗᏐᏍᏛ ᎠᏪᏓᏍᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ. ᏙᎮᏂ ᏍᏊ ᎨᏙᎲ ᏱᎦ ᏢᎮᏂ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏱᎦᏕᎳᏆᏍᎨ. ᎠᎩᏁᎫᏤ ᎠᎮ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏕᏥᎸᏂᎲ. ᎤᎾᏅ ᏧᏂᎩᏒ school Bell Ꭲ ᏧᏭᏂᏅ ᎤᎾᏅ ᏍᏊ bus ᎠᎲ ᎣᏣᏕᏲᎰ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏗᎾᏕᏲᎲᏍᎩ
segments.translation: Rock Fence is where I went. I just went, I wasn’t learning anything! I was mean, beating up the kids. When they moved the school, they moved it to Bell. Also, the teachers used to chase us around the bus.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And they were carrying a stick?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏯᏖᏂ ᎠᏂᏂᏙ ᎠᏎᏃ Ꮭ ᏱᎬᎩᎸᏂᎴ ᏢᎮᏂ ᏱᎬᎩᏂᏱᎮ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꭾ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏂᏥᎦᏛᎲᎾ ᏥᎦ ᏥᎬᏥᏲᎮᎲ
segments.translation: Yeah. They were carrying a board, but they didn’t spank me, ’cause they couldn’t catch me. “That’s why I don’t know anything,” I tell them.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: Gaw, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏥᏣᎴᏅᎲ ᏕᎭᏕᎳᏆᏍᎬ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏭᏍ ᏱᎦ ᎯᏬᏂᏍᎨ?
segments.translation: When you started going to school, was Cherokee all you spoke?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really? The teachers didn’t get onto you?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: yeah, ᏌᏭ Doublehead, Hina Doublehead ᏧᏙᎩᏓ ᏥᏚᏕᏲᏅ Ᏺ ᏯᏓᎸᏂᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏴᎬᏬᏂ. ᎠᏎᎾ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏥᏥᏬᏂᎲ Ᏺ ᎠᏯ ᏥᏣᎳᎩ ᎢᎾ ᎨᎵᎲ ᏄᏓᎴ Ꮕ ᏱᎾᏮᏍᏕ ᏥᏲᏁᎩ ᏱᎨᎮ ᏨᏩᎦᏗ ᏥᎦᏥᏲᎮᎸ
segments.translation: Yeah, one Doublehead. Hiner Doublehead was his name, he taught us. He would spank you if you spoke Cherokee. But me, I was speaking Cherokee. “I’m Cherokee. I would look different if I was White,” I told them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What grade did you finish at?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Probably about fifth.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Fifth, uh-huh.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: That’s about it, I guess.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Then you quit?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yeah. It got too hard for me.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Is that when you two found each other?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎲᎥ, ᎦᎵ four ᏣᏁᎲ ᏗᏪᏥ ᎩᎳ. ᏥᎨᎯᏙᎲᏂ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏎᎾ Ꮭ ᏳᏂᎩᏎ Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏳᏰᏟᏗ ᏯᏩᏕᏟ ᎦᏳᎵ ᎮᎾ ᏧᏅᏘ. ᎠᏯ Ꮕ ᏱᎦᏥᏍᎪᏍᎩ ᏂᎦᎵᏍᏗ Ꮓ ᎤᎾ ᏗᏝ ᎨᎲ
segments.translation: I already had four kids, when we met. I ran him off, too, but he didn’t leave. No use, me hiding it, he already knows. It makes it like I’m lying, that way.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Because you were lying! He never chased you off!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Ꮎ Kenwood ᏣᏁᎲ Ꭰ ᏂᎪᎸ ᏣᏅᏘᏲᎯᎲ ᎠᏂᏁᎵ ᏃᎴ ᎤᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩ Ꮓ ᎠᏂᏁᎵ ᏂᎪᎸᏛ ᏥᏍᎩᏍᎨᎯᏙᎲ ᏥᏫᎾ ᏧᎨᎲ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎾᏅ ᎠᏓᎨᎯᏙᎮ. ᎤᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩᎾ ᏙᏛ ᏣᎯᎷᎬᏅ ᏱᎬᎨᎯᏙᎵ. ᏔᎵ ᎮᏂ ᏂᎦᎦ ᏙᎭ ᎥᎨᎯᏙᎸ ᏴᏗ ᏙᎮᏂ ᎩᎶ ᏣᏓᎨᎯᏐ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏃᎴ ᎩᎶ ᏱᏬᎨᎯᏐ. ᏳᏓᎭ ᎮᏂ ᏙᏳ ᎠᎦᏎᏍᏙᏗ ᎥᎬᏬᏂᎲ
segments.translation: There was a married couple in Kenwood, the husband and wife were always fussing. “You were always chasing me when I was a young man,” he said. And she was chasing him. His wife said, “You always came back, when I chased you off!” It has two different meanings, ain’t it?! If you say “you were chasing me,” it sounds like, “somebody’s chasing you off,” then there’s “you’re chasing something.” Sometimes you have to pay attention to what you’re saying.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎪᎯᏛ ᏥᎦ ᏙᏳᏍᎫ Ꮭ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏯᏂᏬᏂ
segments.translation: Today, children aren’t speaking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ Ᏺ ᏙᏗᎦᏛᏒ Ᏺ ᎠᎦᎵᏃᎮᏗ ᎮᏂ
segments.translation: How we all grew up, we were speaking it to each other.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s all we were speaking.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏣᎳᎩ ᏥᏗᏬᏂᎲ. ᎪᎯᏂ ᏥᎦ Ꮎ Ꮲ ᎨᏍᏓ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏯᏃᏟᎩ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏥᏓᎾᏛᏍᎦ ᏝᏅ ᏯᏃᏟᎩ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏲᏁᎦᎭ ᏭᏅ ᎨᎬᎵᏃᎮᏙ Ꮓ
segments.translation: We were speaking Cherokee. And nowadays, the children don’t understand it. They don’t understand Cherokee. They just talk to them in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᏙᎮᏂ ᎡᏙᏓ--ᎥᎩᏙ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎢᎭ ᎮᏂ ᎣᏍᏗᏬᏂᏍᎩ ᎨᎲ ᏙᎩᎾᏛᏏᏗᏒ ᏧᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ Ꮓ ᏧᏩᏩᎴᏅᎲ Ꮓ ᎾᎯᏳ ᎢᎦ ᏥᎬᎬᏍᎦᎬ ᏗᎾᏕᏲᎲᏍᎦ ᎾᏛ ᎯᎢ ᏄᏍᏓ ᎠᏫ ᏕᎬᏮᏂᏍᏗᎲ. ᎥᎬᏍᎦᎬ ᏣᎳᎩᎭ ᎣᏥᏬᏂᎲ ᏢᏴ Ꮓ ᎤᏣᏘᎾ ᏧᏬᎩᏴᏛᏅ ᎣᏥᏣᎳᎩᎭ Ꮓ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎾᏂᎦᏔᎲᎾ ᏗᏂᏯᎥ ᏥᎨᎰ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎤᎾ ᏬᎩᏴᏛᏅ. Boy ᎤᏟ Ꮫ ᎠᏩᏤᎸᏒ ᎤᎾ ᏧᏥᏯᎥ ᎣᏍᏓ ᏕᏥᏅᏍᎬ ᏲᎩᏍᏆᎸᎡᎵ ᎣᎩᎪᎵᏰᏍᎬ test ᏣᏅᏗᎰ ᏃᏫᏛ Ꮎ Ᏼ ᏱᎩᏓ ᏥᏆᏍᏛᏙ ᎠᏬᏠ ᏢᏴᏃ ᏩᏩᏛᏛ Ꭶ ᎠᏪᎵᏒ. ᎫᏍᏗ Ꮕ ᏃᏥᎦᏔᎲᏂ ᏦᏥᏯ ᎠᏪᎵᏒ Ꮓ ᎡᎵᏗ ᏄᎵᏍᏛᏅ ᏃᎴ ᏥᏍᎪᎵ
segments.translation: Really. Me and my sister, we spoke it growing up. When I started school, the teachers weren’t letting me speak Cherokee. They were hitting me like this [gestures]. They were scolding us for speaking Cherokee. Then eventually, they put us Cherokees in one room. They put us in where they said [was the] “They don’t know anything” classroom. Boy, I was really proud to be in there, myself. I was making good grades, when they gave us a test. I felt like I had a big head. Then I remembered, “We’re in the room where no one knows anything!” Then my head went down.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎡᎳᏗ Ꮫ ᎣᏣᎢᏐ ᎨᎲ ᎠᎬᏱ ᏙᎦᏕᎳᏆᎡᏂ Ꮓ ᎪᎢ ᎮᏂ ᏣᏩᎴᏅ ᎠᎮᏂ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏚᏂᏁᏟᏴᏒ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏛᏗᏝ cave springs, greasy, cave springs ᏗᏝ ᎯᏯ ᏧᎬᏬᎮᎸ ᏃᎴ ᎤᎾ ᏗᏝ. ᎤᎾᏴ ᎣᏤᏙᎲ beaver gap ᏛᏃ ᏃᏥᎦ ᎤᎾ ᏦᏥᏁᎸ ᎡᎳᏓ ᏦᏤᎬ school Ꭲ cave springs Ꮲ ᏗᎳᏑᎶ ᏱᏙᎩᎾᎡ Ꮩ ᏙᎬᎳᏑᏢᏂ ᎣᏤᎬ school Ꭲ ᏃᎴ ᏳᏓᎭᏅ ᏙᏨᏟᎣ ᎨᎲ ᏅᏱ ᎬᏗ. ᏦᏣᎢᏒ Ꮎ ᎠᏂᏲᏁᎦ yeah
segments.translation: We walked to school. I started at Greasy. Then they changed and sent us to Cave Springs from Greasy. “You’re going to Cave Springs,” they told me. Where we’re at now, Beaver Gap, that’s where we lived. Then we would walk to Cave Springs. We didn’t have shoes; we walked to school barefoot. Sometimes we would have rock fights as we were going down the road with the white kids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: Soldier, ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᏒ ᏕᏣᏕᏅᏍᎨᏍ ᎢᎦ ᎢᏣᎵᏍᏓᏴᏗ ᎤᏂᎾᏌᎡᎨ ᏧᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ?
segments.translation: Soldier, back then, did you pack a lunch to school? Or did the school have food?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Huh-uh, no.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: We had to pack lunches.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏳᏓᎭ Ꮫ ᎠᎪᏂ ᏬᏤᏙᎲ Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏲᏥᏫᏗᎮ ᎣᎩᎩᏍᏗ ᏳᏓᎭ ᎦᏚ ᏙᏥᏫᏗᎲ. ᏙᏍᎫ ᎦᏚ ᎤᏱᎦ sandwich Ꮎ ᏲᎪᏢᎾᏁᎵ ᏙᏥᏫᏗᎰ ᎣᎩᎩᏍᏗ. ᏳᏓᎭᏅ ᎠᎪᏂᏭ
segments.translation: Sometimes we just starved, because we didn’t have anything to take to eat. Sometimes we took bread. Also, sometimes we took sandwiches if they fixed them for us. Sometimes we just went without food.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, starvation.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎾᎮᏂ beaver gap ᏥᎦ ᎤᎾ ᎮᏂ ᏦᏥᏁᎸ ᎾᎯᏳ
segments.translation: Back then, we lived at Beaver Gap.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: By the dam?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: Ꭵ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏗᏟᎤ. ᎠᎬᏱ ᎠᏩᏕᏅ ᎤᎾᎮᏂ ᎠᏩᏕᏅ ᎠᏎᎾ Ꮟ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏗᏝᎤᏴ ᎠᏓᏁᎸ ᎤᎾ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏩᏕᏅ ᎠᏩᏕᏂᏢ ᏁᎵᏍᎪ ᎾᏕᏘᏱ ᏥᎨᎲ yeah
segments.translation: Yeah, this [gestures] way. When I was first born, it was there. But it was near there, the house. That’s where I was born. It was 80 years ago, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏙᏛ Ꭰ ᎭᏩᏘ ᎥᎩᏙ ᏙᎩᎾᏛᏏᏗᏒ water gravy Ꭴ ᏱᎦ ᏦᏍᏗᎩᏍᎬ ᏌᎾᎴ ᏱᎦ
segments.translation: Really … when me and my sister were growing up, all we ate was water gravy in the morning.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎠᏯ Ꮫ ᏳᏓᎭ Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏲᏥᎩᏍᎨ ᏬᎩᎨᎯᏙᎲ school Ꭲ ᏗᏝ
segments.translation: Us, sometimes we weren’t eating anything when they ran us off to school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then flour…

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Really, we were there, hungry, sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏃᎴᏅ ᎡᎵᏭ ᏦᎩᎲ ᎢᏌ ᎦᏚ ᎡᎵᏭ ᏙᎬᏳᏩᏂᏍᏙᏗ ᏃᎴ water gravy ᏃᎴ ᎦᏚ biscuit ᏙᏳ ᎤᏖᏗ ᎠᎩᏍᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: Sometimes we had flour for her to make bread with. Then water gravy and biscuits. It was really good to eat.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏍᎩᏭ Ꮫ ᎤᏣᏘ Ꮟ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᎠᏑᏍᏗ ᎦᏚ ᎢᎾ.
segments.translation: Today, water biscuits and gravy are still really good to eat.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Yeah

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Ain't it?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: you bet. ᎠᏯ Ꮫ ᏍᎫ ᎤᏠᏱ biscuit
segments.translation: You bet. It’s the same for me, biscuits.

segments.speaker: carolyn-fourkiller
segments.translation: I like biscuits.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: And gravy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏎᏃ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᏥᏓᏅᏛᏍᎦ Ꮭ ᏱᎬᏂᎦ
segments.translation: But these kids, today, won’t eat it.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏙᏳᏗ ᏍᎫ Ꮭ I don’t want it ᏯᏅᏓ ᎡᎵᏭ
segments.translation: Really. They will say, “I don’t want it.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎤᏂᎩᏒᎢᏛ gravy ᏱᎨᎪᏢᎾᏁᎵ Ꭰ ᎤᏅᏗ ᎠᏅᏗᏍᎪ ᏃᏭᏅ ᎠᎹ ᏱᎦᏛᎾ Ꮓ that’s not gravy ᏯᏅᏗ ᎮᏃ ᎤᏅᏗ ᏄᏓᏠᏯᏍᏛᏂ ᏱᎦ yeah. Ꭰ ᏗᏣᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᏒ Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎤᏂᏃᎮᏢ ᏱᎨᏎ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎤᏪᏘ ᏥᏛᏳᎾᏂᎩᏒ ᎠᏂᏣᎳᎩ Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎣᎾᏛᎦᏅ ᏱᎨᏎ ᎠᏂᏃᎮ ᏍᎬ ᏗᏣᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: They’re used to the gravy they make for them today with milk. Now, if you use water, they’ll say, “That’s not gravy,” ’cause there’s no milk in it. Your parents, did they ever talk about the old Cherokees who came from the old place? You all haven’t heard any stories from your parents?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎢᎦᏗᏛ ᎥᎩᏙ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏳᎾᏝᏃᎮᏟ ᎠᏂᏃᎮᏍᎪ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ. ᎠᏎᏃ Ꮭ ᎤᎪᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏯᏩᏅᏘ ᎫᏍᏗ. ᏍᎫ ᎢᎦ Ꮕ Ꭵ sally mink ᎮᏂ ᏚᏙᎡ ᎤᎵᏌ ᎠᎬᏴᎳ ᎠᎩᎯᏅᏍᏊ ᏣᎦᏟᎶᏍᏛᏅ
segments.translation: Some. My brother and my dad, when they talked, that’s what they talked about. But I don’t know too much about it. All I know is that Sally Mink, she was one of his great-grandmothers. I have one of her pictures.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be!

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: And she was blind!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏍᎩᎾ ᎧᏃᎮᏢᏍᎬ, ᎤᏃᎮᏢᏅ ᎧᏃᎮᏢᏍᎪ ᏥᎨᎲ. ᎠᎯᏂ ᎠᎮᏂ ᎠᏂᏥᎩᎵ ᏕᎧᏃᎮᏍᎬ Ᏺ. ᏒᏃᏱ ᎠᏁᏙ ᏥᏓᏃᏎ. ᎡᏂᏏ ᎢᎾ ᎠᎾᏗᎰ ᎨᎮ ᎠᏂᏃᎮᏍᎪ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎡᏙᏓ ᎾᏅ ᎤᏙ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎣᎩᎾᏛᏓᏍᏙ ᎠᏯ ᎾᎠ ᏫᏙᎩᏂᏠ ᎡᎳᏗ Ꮎ ᎠᏂᏥᎩᎵ ᎮᏂ ᎤᏓᏂᎵ ᏱᎦᏂᎩ Ꮲ ᎠᏂᏥᎩᎵ ᎤᎾᏕᏙᏗ ᏣᎾᏗᏍᎪ ᎠᏗᏍᎨ ᎠᏅᏗᎲ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏂᏃᎮᏍᎬ ᎠᏓᏁᎸ ᎮᏂ Ꮎ corner ᏅᎩ ᏧᏂᏍᏗ ᎠᏂᏥᎩᎵ ᎤᎾᎩᎶ ᎤᏛᏅ ᏭᏛᏅᏂ ᎯᎢ ᏂᎬᏅ ᎤᎾ ᎤᎩᎶ ᏍᎾ ᏥᎭᏬᏍᏗ ᏣᎵᎦᎵᏎᎪ ᎧᏬᎵᏕᏍᎬ ᎤᏓᏂᎵ ᎠᏍᏘᏰᏅ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏂᏄᏗᎰ Ꭿ ᏄᏍᏓ ᎠᏂᏄᏓᏁᎰ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏗᏝ ᏂᏛᏳᎩᎳ ᏧᎾᏒᏁᏏ ᎠᎭᏂᎾ ᏗᏝ Ꮠ ᎾᎯᏳ ᎮᏂ
segments.translation: She was the one that was telling about it. They talked about what she used to talk about. They just mostly talked about boogers. The ones that come out at midnight, they call them. They called her “enisi.” They were talking about her, my dad and his sister. That’s who we were listening to, we were sitting there on the floor. “‘These boogers [come], when somebody is in bed, sick. They say these boogers bother them,’ she said,” he said. That’s what they were saying when they were talking about it. “‘On the house, the corner, there were four little boogers perched,’ she said. ‘The biggest one, that’s where it had a place, sitting. That’s when the sick person has trouble breathing. They used the hair and wrapped it around here [gestures] and there [gestures] and when they pull it, that’s when they have trouble breathing. The sick person,’ that’s what she said, telling whoever was listening to her.” My dad’s brother, Tsal(i) was his name. He was sitting nearby, too, listening to the old woman. “How do you know what the boogers were doing? Is that what you do, too?” he said to her. “You be quiet! You are asking rude questions!” she said to him. She scolded him for talking about her.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏣᎵᎦᎵᏎᎪ ᎧᏬᎵᏕᏍᎬ ᎠᏗᎮᏅ ᎧᏃᎮᏢᏍᎬ ᏕᎧᏃᏎᎮ ᎨᏥᏃᏎᎸᏍᎬ Ꭱ Ꮂ ᎡᏙᏓ ᎢᎾ ᏗᎾᏓᏅᏟ ᏣᎵ ᏚᏙ Ꭱ. ᎾᎠ ᎤᏬᏞ ᏍᎫ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎧᏃᎮᏢᏍᎨ Ꮎ ᎠᎬᏴᎵᎨ. “ᏙᎲ ᏂᎯ ᎢᏣᏗ ᎾᏅᏛᏁᎲ ᎠᏂᏥᎩᎳ ᏣᏗ ᏍᎩᎨ ᏅᏕᏃᎰ ᏍᎫ ᏂᎯ?” ᎠᏓᏙᏎᎮ Ꮎ ᎠᏧᏣ. “ᎯᏑᎳᎪ ᏂᎯ ᎡᏍᎨ ᏍᎬᏛᏍᎩ” ᎠᎪᏎᎮ ᎠᏥᏍᎦᎨ ᎠᏓᏃᎮᏍᎬ Ꮎ ᎠᏧᏣ ᎣᏂᏭ ᎠᎯᎵᏎ Ꭱ ᏙᏗᎰᏂ ᎠᏕᎵᎾ ᎩᎶ ᏱᏣᏙᎸᎡᎵᏟ Ꭰ ᏳᏫᎶ ᏘᎨᏫᎾ ᎭᏗᎰ ᎠᏓᏙᏎᎮ. ᎠᎦᏐᎮᎮ Ꮎ ᎠᏧᏣ ᏍᎩ ᎾᏓᏪᏎᎲ ᎤᏔᏲᏢᏅ ᏱᎦ ᏱᏲᎩ Ꮓ ᏱᏣᎷᏥ ᏳᏫᎥᏏ ᎠᏩᏅᏘᏅ ᎠᏯ ᏙᎨ ᎠᏯ ᏥᎦᏍᏘᏁᎪ ᏅᏬᏘ ᏱᏣᏯᎴᏂ ᎢᎾᎨ? ᏱᎪᏩᏘᏅ ᏨᏑᏅ ᏰᎦ ᎠᏓᏙᏎᎮ. ᏂᎪᎸ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᎦᏘᏂᏙᎮ ᏅᏬᏘ ᎧᎾᏍᏕᏟᏍᎩ Ꭱ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꮕ ᏭᎯᎶᏞ ᎠᏗᎲ Ꮎ ᏁᏗ ᏥᏍᏆ ᏧᏙᎩᏗ ᏤᎮ. Ned
segments.translation: The boy was right behind her, just talking. “When somebody comes to borrow money, you walk off. And you say you’re blind!” he said. She scolded him for saying that to her. “When you come back, you bring the amount they asked for! I know it. So why do you take me with you to get medicines in the woods? You can see, you can go by yourself!” he said. She always took him to cut roots for her. That’s how it came to be. That Ned Bird, he was called. Ned…

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: Long Bird

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ned Long Bird ᏣᏃᏎᎲ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏅᏘ Ned Bird Ꭴ ᏱᎦ ᏱᏚᏙ ᎨᎲ ᏁᏗ ᏥᏍᏆ Ꮭ ᎩᎶ ᏱᎬᏩᏅᏘ ᏳᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᎨᎲ Ned ᎠᏯ ᏥᏕᎯ. ᎠᏥᏃᏢ ᎮᏂ ᎤᏛᏅ ᎠᏗᎲ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎠᏓᎨ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎠᏥᏁᎮ Ned ᎨᏥᎢᎶᏟ. ᎠᏥᎢᎶᏢ ᎮᏂ ᎨᎮ Ꮎ ᎠᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᎤᎾ ᎮᏂ ᎤᏖᎵᏛ. ᎠᏗᏍᎪ ᎨᎲ Ꮂ ᏥᎪᎥ ᏱᎦ ᎣᏥᎪ ᏱᎦ Ꮓ ᏍᎫ ᏂᎦ picture ᏥᎬᏓ ᏓᏁᎸ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎤᏩᏏ
segments.translation: Ned Longbird they called him. I don’t know if his name was just Ned Bird or Longbird. Nobody knew how old Ned was. Us, here now. He was brought here, he said. He was a baby when they came on the Trail of Tears. An old lady was carrying him, he joined her. That’s what they said, we haven’t seen her, all we have is that picture on the wall at the house.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏅᎡ Ned Longbird ᏣᏗ ᏂᎪᎸ ᎠᏨᏏᏰᏍᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏅᏃ. ᏂᎪᎸ ᏳᏍᏚᏭ ᎨᎲ Ꮭ ᏯᎯ ᎫᏖᏍᎬ ᏍᎫ ᎭᎳ ᏍᎫ ᏱᏄᏗᏝᎦ. ᎤᏔᏂ Ꮫ ᎦᏒᎴᏂ ᏳᏄᏫ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᏝᏅᏂ. ᎤᎾᏅ ᎡᏍᏗᏝ ᏦᏥᏁᎸ ᏳᎷᏥ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏱᏙᎩᏃᏟ ᏏᏲ ᏯᎪᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ ned ᏯᎩᏠᏏᎦ porch Ꭲ ᎧᏦᏕ ᏳᏩᏴᎭ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏯᏝᎯ ᎦᏚ ᎴᏱᎦ ᎤᏘᏴ ᏯᏝ table Ꭲ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏂᎦᏓ ᏱᏕᎦᏢᎦ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏴᎬᏂᏅᎪ ᏯᏂᎦ ᏥᎨᎲ. Yeah ᎢᎮᏙᎸ ᏯᎪᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ. ᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏥᏄᏍᏓ ᏁᏗ ᏥᏍᏆ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏙᎮᏂ ᎣᏍᏓ ᎮᏂ ᎤᏔᎾ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎠᎬᏴᎵ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎣᏍᏓ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᏨᏏᏰᏗ ᏅᏃ. ᏳᏍᏗᏭᎨ ᏱᎫᏖᎩ ᏳᎪ ᏅᏃ Ꮲ ᎠᎲ ᏍᎫ ᎦᏢᏍᎬ ᎤᏝᏩᏛ ᎦᏒᎴᏂ ᏂᎪᎸ ᎤᏔᏂ ᎦᏒᎴᏂ ᎤᏄᏩ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: That Ned Longbird she’s talking about, he was always walking on the road. He was always picking up anything on the road, no matter how hot it was! And he’d have on a big coat. He’ll have things in a bag. We lived nearby and when he came and we’d be sitting, my late father would say hello. Ned would come up to the porch and go inside the house. If there was something there, like bread, he would take it all and come back out and go on. [laughter] “Yeah, come back again!” Dad would tell him. That’s how Ned Longbird was. He was a good person and he was old, but he was walking good on the road. He would pick anything up on the road and put it in his pocket ’cause he had on a big coat all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was a searcher, wasn’t he?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: yeah, ᏱᏩᏴᎯᏭ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎦᎵᏦᏕ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏳᏩᏛ kitchen Ꭲ ᏗᏝ ᎠᎩᏍᏓ ᏯᏂᎦ ᏥᎨᎲ. ᎡᎮᏙᎸ ᏯᎪᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: Yeah, he would go in the house. If he found something to eat in the kitchen, he would take it and put it in his pocket, then he’d leave again. They’d tell him, “Come again!”

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: Lillie Ꮎ ᏣᏂᎦᏔᎲ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮕ ᏅᏬᏘ ᎤᎾᏍᏕᏟ ᏱᎦ ᏚᏂᏑᏩᏍᎬ ᏱᎦ Ꮲ ᎴᏱᎦ ᏚᏁᏍᏓᏁᎲ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᏢᏅ ᏫᏄᎵᏍᏛᏂ ᏓᎭ ᏍᎩᎾ
segments.translation: Lillie, those ones that knew things about root medicine, like, for coughing or if they’re in pain. Nowadays, it’s not used anymore, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Me, I still use it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Still?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: The ones I know, I look for them and use them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᎤᎵᏍᎨᏗ Ꭱ ᏍᎩ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏴᎦᏔᎭ. ᏱᏓᏤᏞ ᏍᏗ ᏯᎩᎦᏙᎣᏎ ᎨᎵᏍᎪ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᎫᏍᏗ
segments.translation: It’s good to know those things. Nowadays, I think it would be better if I had learned those things.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: yeah, ᎣᏍᏗ ᏛᏲ ᎤᏝᏂᎩᏗ ᎮᏂ ᏅᏬᏘ ᎢᎾᎨ ᏂᏓᏳᎶᏒ. ᎾᏅ ᎦᏅᎦᏘ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏱᏣᎵᏍᏓᏁ ᏳᏣᎷᏥ ᏅᏬᏘ ᏰᏣᏁᎵ. ᎯᏂᏴ ᎢᎮᏙᎸᎢ ᏰᏦᎮᎵ ᏱᏫᏤᏙᎵᏅ ᏰᏣᎪᎵᏰ ᎣᏍᏓ Ꮫ ᏝᏃ ᏅᏬᏘ ᏱᎦᏰᏨᏏ ᎾᏅ Ᏺ ᎢᎾᎨ ᎡᎯ ᏱᎦ Ᏺ keep drinking it ᏂᎪᎸ ᏂᎦᏗ ᏩᎵᏒᎲᏍᎩ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏨᏢᎬ. ᎾᏅ ᏱᏛᎠᎵᏂᏌᏂ ᎦᏅᎦᏘ ᎤᎾᏓᏁᎸ. ᏌᏭ ᏭᏅ ᏱᎾᏅᏓᎲᏏ
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s good. And the medicine is strong, that came from the woods. Now, the doctors, when something is wrong, you go and they give you medicine. They’ll tell you, “Come back again, at this time.” You go back, and they check you and say, “You’re alright.” And they won’t give you medicine again. But the medicine from the woods, keep drinking it all the time, until it’s all gone, if you’re sick. But what the doctor gave you, the sickness will start again. And the doctors will only give you medicine one time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: yeah,ᏙᏛ Ꭰ ᏥᏃᎮᏍᎬ ᎪᎯ ᎠᏂᏥᎩᎳ Ꮭ ᎠᎸᎯᏳ ᎤᏂᏃᎮᏢ ᏱᎨᎲ ᏴᏫ ᏧᎾᏍᏗ
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true. … You were talking about boogers. Did they ever talk about little people?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: I’ve heard about the little people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏢᎮ ᎠᎸᎯ ᏘᎦᏙᎥᏒ ᏱᎨᎮ Ꮭ ᎠᎸᎯᏳ ᎦᎯᎪᎥ ᏱᎨᎮ?
segments.translation: You’ve never interacted with them? Or you’ve never seen them?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎲᎥ, ᎲᏲ ᎠᎸᎯᏳ ᎦᏥᎪᎥ ᏱᎦ. ᎠᏂᏃᎮᏍᎬᏪ Ꭰ ᎤᏟᏗᏝ ᏣᏁᎲ ᏴᏫ
segments.translation: No, I’ve never seen them. They were just talking about them, the people that lived by us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎢᎦᏓ ᎮᏂ ᏙᏳ ᎠᏂᏬᏂ ᎤᎾᏛᎦᏅ ᏱᎨᏐ ᏳᏂᏃᎮᏟ
segments.translation: Some people who talk about them have just heard stories about them.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: All I know is that they say, “They will get you lost.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right. That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: When the little people catch you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎡᏘᏴ ᏥᎨᏒ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏩᏓᏗᏍᎩᎪ Ꭸ ᏫᏣᏅᏓᏗᏍᎪ ᎴᏱᎦ ᎡᏘᏴ ᏥᎨᏒ Ꮭ ᏱᏙᏧᎾᏓᏂᎳ ᎦᏚᎩ ᏣᏁᎪ?
segments.translation: Do you all remember how it was a long time ago, when somebody got sick, everybody went to help out?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏧᏓᏁᏍᏕᎸᎯᏙᎰ ᏝᎦ, ᎩᎶ ᎴᏱᎦ ᏁᎲᏂ ᏱᏄᎵᏍᏛᏂ ᏣᏁᎬ Ꮓ ᏣᏂᏨᏙᏩᏍᎪ ᏃᎴ
segments.translation: They would help out. Or, when somebody died, everybody went over there to help out. And some would spend the night there.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: They would sit outside.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: yeah, ᏙᏯ ᏗᏝ ᏃᎴᏅ ᎠᎾᏓᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩ ᎨᎲ ᎢᎦᏗ ᎠᏂᏍᎦᏴ Ꮎ ᏙᏯᏗᏝ ᏯᏂᏙᎾ ᏯᎾᎵᏍᎪᏅᎲᏍᎩ ᎨᏒ ᎾᎯᏳ ᎫᏍᏗ
segments.translation: Yeah, on the porch. And some were there to cook. And then the men will be standing around talking or telling lies.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Ꮫ ᎡᎵ ᏄᏠᏯᏍᏛᏂ ᎦᏱᎪᎩ. “ᎤᏝᏂᎩᏗ ᎮᏂ ᎦᏱᎪᎩ!” ᎦᏥᏲᏎᎰ “ᏱᏣᎵᏍᎪᏂ ᎮᏂ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏂᎯ ᎥᎬᏱ ᎣᏍᏓ ᏱᏂᏣᎵᏍᏓᏏ ᏚᏳᎦᏛ ᎡᎯᏃᎮᏍᎨᏍᏗ ᏰᏣᎳᏏᏓ!”
segments.translation: Yeah, there always has to be lies. “It’s a strong thing; telling lies,” I tell them. “When you a tell a lie, something good will happen to you! But if you tell the truth, they will not believe you!”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏎᎾ ᏍᎩ ᏥᏄᏍᏓ ᏣᏂᏃᎮᏢᏍᎪ ᎠᏂᏍᎬᏯ ᎪᏛ ᎾᎠ ᎧᏫ ᏣᎾᏚᎩᏍᎪ. ᏩᏅᏔᏗᏍᎪᎨ ᏳᏓᎭ ᏍᎩ ᏄᎾᏛᏁᎵᏙᎸ ᏂᏣᏛᏁᎵᏙᎸ ᎴᏱᎦ ᎭᏓᏅᏖᏍᎬ ᏳᏓᎭ ᏪᏙᎰ ᏃᎴ ᏗᏛᏓᏩᏛᎯᏙ ᏥᎨᏒ ᎮᏍᏓ
segments.translation: But that’s how it was. The men would sit outside, telling things, sitting by the fire. And drinking coffee. Do you remember, sometimes, you doing that, or you all doing that? Do you sometimes go back there, while you’re thinking about it? And then how we all used to visit each other? It wasn’t…

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᏑᏒᎯᏓᏅ, ᎠᏫᏳ ᎪᎯᎾ ᏥᎦ ᎢᎾᏅ ᏱᎦ ᎩᎳ ᏑᏒᎯᏓ ᏳᏮᏗ ᎩᎶ ᏳᏮᏩᏛᎯᏓ ᎾᏅ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎡᎳᏓ ᏭᏴ ᏫᎦᎷᎯᏍᏗ ᏱᏗᎦᏁᎵ ᏳᏬᏒ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏗᎦᏃᏨᏟ ᎮᏂ ᏧᏙᎩᏓ ᏥᎬᏁᎸ ᎤᏛᎯᏍᏓ ᎠᏯᏅ ᎦᏚᏌ ᎢᎾ ᎤᎨᏛᎵᏴ ᎦᏚᏏ ᏥᏛᏲᏤᎲ. ᎤᎾ ᏦᏤᎬ ᎣᎩᏥ ᏂᎦᏓ ᏑᏒᎯᏓ ᏧᏬᏤᏙᎲ. ᎢᏣᏂᎮᏍᏗ ᏳᎾᏛᏂ ᏬᎩᏒᎯᎰ ᏧᏐᏩᎸᏗᏅ ᏧᏙᎩᏓ ᎠᏍᎬᏯ ᏤᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꮎ ᏗᎦᏃᏣᏟ ᎤᏪᏥ Lillie ᎤᏛᎾ ᎠᎭᏂᏭ ᏕᏂᎾᎨᏍᏗ ᏥᏔᎦ ᎠᏨᏯ ᎢᎾ ᎠᎾᏙᎯᏒ ᎠᏭ ᎦᎸᎳᏗᏝ ᎤᎾᎩᎴᏍᏗ ᏂᏗᏣᏗᎩᏒᏂᏭᏅ ᏱᎦ. Ꭽ! ᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᎾᎠ Ꮫ ᏫᏥᏅᎪ ᎦᏁᎵᏥᏝ ᎢᎾ ᎤᏑᎸ ᎲᏍᎫ ᏱᏚᎳᏑᎴᏎᏭ ᎦᏁᎵᏥᏝ ᎤᏑᎸ ᏙᏍᏂᎪ ᏧᏐᏩᎸᏗ ᏙᏂᏍᎫ ᏌᎾᎴ ᏥᏔᎦ ᏧᏙᎯᏒ. ᎤᎾ ᎦᎾᎸ Ꭿ ᏄᏍᏛ Ꮎ Ꮭ ᏱᎫᏝᎡ sheetrock Ꮎ ᏥᏕᎫᏝᎣ ᎦᎾᎸ ᎤᎾ ᏥᎬᏙᎬ ᏥᏅᎬ ᏥᏳᎩᏓ ᎠᏩᏗᏛᎲ. ᏙᏛᏩᏗᎩᏏᏅ ᎠᏪᎵᏒ ᏥᏔᎦ ᎤᏬᏟᏗᏅ ᎤᏂᏰᎸᏒ ᎢᎬᎩᏰᏓᏍᏗᎲ
segments.translation: It would be all night! Nowadays, it has to be far away before you can spend the night. Back then, if they lived in walking distance, you would spend the night. There was an old man named Diganotsatl(i) who lived there. We lived way up on the hill from him. We would go there with our mom. We would spend the night. When they said, “You all spend the night here!” we would spend the night. There was a man named Tsusolvd(i). He was Diganotsatl(i)’s son. He said, “Lillie! Let’s just lie here! If the rooster crows, it’ll be sitting right above us! I just hope it don’t poop on you!” he said. “Haw!” I told him. I was laying real close to him, him with his overalls on. He didn’t even take his overalls off. Me and Tsusolvd(i) were in bed. And then in the morning, the rooster crowed. There was a board across there, because there was no wall, just sheetrock. That’s where the rooster was standing, right above where I was laying. I got up. I thought it was going to poop on me! They thought it was funny, and they laughed at me.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏌᏭ ᏳᏩᎦᏗ Ꭿ ᏥᏕᎦᏃᎮ Ꭿ ᏗᎦᏃᏣᏟ ᏣᏂᏁᎸ ᏢᏂ ᏍᎫ ᏥᏙᏛᏄᏪᏍᎪ ᎢᎦᏂᏢᏗ ᏱᎦ ᎮᏍᏗ ᎮᏂ ᏍᎩ ᏱᏄᏅᏍᏕ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏙᎬᏩᎾᏄᏭ ᎮᏂ ᎤᎾᏂᎲ. ᏱᏩᎵᏍᏛᏡᏂ ᏱᏭᎾᏏᏅ ᎴᏱ ᏍᎫ ᎮᏂ ᎨᎲ. ᏍᎫ ᏄᏍᏛ ᏃᎴ ᏱᏭᎾᏗᏛᏁᏏ ᏱᏚᏂᏰᏥ ᎦᏥᏯᏅᏛᏗᎲ ᎨᎲ ᏥᏛᏂᏁᎸ ᎨᏴ ᎨᏓᎵ
segments.translation: One time, that Diganotsatl(i) she was talking about, they lived there. Back then, we didn’t take our clothes off to go to bed, like they do now. If I sat down somewhere, that’s where I slept. That’s how it was. When they got up, when they woke up, [laughter] […] down the hill.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.translation: Because all of them…

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᏕᎰᏂ ᏍᎫ ᏳᏓᎭ ᏍᎩ ᏃᎬᏍᏛ Ꭸ ᎡᏍᏗᏝ ᏦᏥᏁᎸ ᎦᏅᏓᏗ ᏳᏓᎭᏂ ᏙᏯ ᎮᏂ ᎣᏥᎳᎨᏲ ᏥᎨᎲ porch ᎪᎩ ᎡᏍᎦ ᏗᏝ ᏥᎦᏁᎸ Ꮎ Nellie Mays ᏥᎨᎲ ᏧᏙᎩᏓ ᎾᏅ Gill Fay Mayes ᏥᏚᏙᎥ ᎠᏂᏁᎵ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꮕ ᏙᎨᏰᏍᏗᏍᎪ ᏙᏗᏝ ᎣᏥᎳᎨᏲ ᏌᎾᎴ. ᏌᎾᎴ ᏱᎦᏙᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᎩᎸᏗ “Wake up, wake up!” ᏯᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ “Time to get up!” ᏯᏗ Gill Fay Mayes.
segments.translation: That’s how we were something. We lived closer this way. I remember, sometimes we were all scattered laying, sleeping outside on the porch in the summer. This [gestures] way lived the late Nellie Mays. She lived there with her husband, Gill Mayes. That’s who would wake us up on the porch in the mornings. He’d be there early in the morning, on horseback. “Wake up, wake up!” he’d say. “Time to get up!” he’d say. Gill Fay Mayes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You all got aggravated with him?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: He would wake us up from sleeping.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all would get aggravated sometimes?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏳᏓᎭ Ꭱ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏥᎾᏆᏘᎲ ᏍᎫ ᎣᎩᏰᏍᏗᎲ
segments.translation: Yeah, sometimes I hated him for waking us up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏙᏛ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏙᏯ ᏗᏝ ᎢᎩᏒᎯᎭ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: That’s true, back then, we all slept outside.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: yeah, ᏙᏯ ᏗᏝ. ᎮᏍᏓ ᎮᏂ ᎰᏩ ᎦᎵᏦᏕ ᏙᏯ Ꮫ ᎣᏥᎳᎨᏲ ᎨᎲ porch Ꭲ
segments.translation: Yeah, outside. We weren’t inside all that much. We were all scattered around outside on the porch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎯᏅ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᎡᎵᏭ ᎩᎶ ᏴᏓᏍᎫᏯ ᎥᎬᏟᎲ ᏙᎭ?
segments.translation: But nowadays, somebody will hit you on the head while you’re sleeping. Ain’t it?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏙᏛ ᏍᎫ ᎩᎶ ᏯᏓᏴᏨᏂᎦ ᏙᏯ ᏴᎦᏟᎭ
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right. Someone will hit you in the throat, if you’re sleeping outside.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎯᏅ ᏓᏨᏯᏛᏛᏂ ᏛᏍᎪᎸᏥᏭᏍ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎬᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎢᎨᏒ ᎢᏤᎵ ᏙᎨ ᏴᏛᏂ ᎯᎸᏍᎩ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᏩᏟᎶᏢ ᏫᏛᏍᎪᎸᏥᏍ ᎮᎵ?
segments.translation: I’m going to ask you all this: is it going to fade away, the Cherokee language? What do you all think? You could say, in a few years it’s going to fade away, is that what you think?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏫᏂᏓᎦᎵᏍᏓᏂᏟ ᎢᏛᎮ Ꮩ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏥᎦᏗ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ Ꮓ ᎣᏂ ᏥᏓᏅᏛᏍᎩ ᏢᏅ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏯᏃᏟᎩ ᎠᏲᏁᎦᎭᏂ ᎠᏯᏅ ᏗᏩᏤᎵ ᏔᎵᏁ ᎥᎩᎵᏏ ᏣᏁᎯ
segments.translation: It’s really going to happen that way. These children that are growing up today, they don’t understand it. All they know is English, my great-grandkids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s all English.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: I don’t know if they understand Cherokee. It’s just English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏂᎾ Ꮩ ᎮᎵᎰ? ᏛᎵᏒᏂᎨ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎦᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎨᏒ? ᏙᎨ ᎠᎢᏎᏗᏭ?
segments.translation: And how about you? What do you think? Is it just going to end, to speak Cherokee? Or will it keep going?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎦᏳᎵᏛ ᎤᎪᏗ ᎤᎵᏒᏂ. ᏢᏂ ᏱᎬᏃᏟᎩ Ꮎ ᎠᏂᏐ ᎣᏂ ᏥᏚᎾᏛᏏᏓ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏱᏛᏝᏃᎮᏛᏂ
segments.translation: A lot of it is already gone. They can’t understand, the ones who are growing up now, when you talk to them in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎯᎾ ᏥᏓᏅᏕᎳᏆ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏥᏓᏁᏲᎲᏍᎩ ᏥᏓᎾᏕᎳᏆ ᎡᎵᏭᎨ ᏛᏳᎵᏍᏕᏝᏙᏛᏂ ᎡᎵᏭ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎦᏬᏂᏍᎩ ᎨᎲ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏩᏟᎶᏢ
segments.translation: How about these children that are learning here? The ones that are being taught, that are learning, do you think it’s going to help them to speak Cherokee eventually?

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: Yeah, ᎡᎵᏭᏅ ᏧᎾᏔᏂ ᎨᎮᏍᏗ ᏣᎳᎩ Ꮟ ᎠᏂᏬᏂᎮᏍᏗ ᏱᏫᏚᎾᏓᏘᏅᏂᏅ ᏃᎴ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏱᏚᎾᏟᏃᎮᏗ ᎠᏎᎾ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎠᏂᏬᏂᏍᎦ ᎨᎮᏍᏗ. ᎠᎮᏂ ᏲᏁᎦᎭ ᏭᏂ ᎤᏟᏱᎦ ᎨᎰ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᎤᎾᏭ ᎨᏒ
segments.translation: Probably will, yeah. When they are grown, they will speak Cherokee. And when they have children, if they speak to them in Cherokee, they will be speaking Cherokee. But all it is today, is English.

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᏥᎬᏗ, ᏲᏁᎦᎭᏭᏅ ᏚᎾᏝᏃᎮᏙ Ꮭ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏥᏗᏬᏂ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎮᏂ ᎡᎬᎵᏃᎮᏛ ᎠᎫᏏ Ꮕ ᏍᏊ ᎥᏮᏢᏃᎮᏗᎲ ᎠᏯ ᎧᎵ ᎮᏂ ᎠᎫᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎡᏥ ᎡᏚᏓ Ꮕ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾᏅ ᎫᏌᎭ ᎠᏮᏢᏃᎮᏗᎲ ᎡᏙᏗ ᏅᎨᎲ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏗᏩᏛᏏ ᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏍᏗ ᏲᏁᎦ ᏥᎪᎵᎪ Ꮓ ᏧᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ ᎮᏂ ᏣᏩᎴᏅ ᎩᎳ ᎤᎾ ᏩᏮᏕᎳᏆᎥ ᏲᏁᎦ ᏚᏙᎥ ᏄᏍᏗᏓᏅ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᎬᏱ Ꮭ ᎯᎮᏂ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᏙᎮᏂ ᏢᎮᏂ hᎡᏂ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏯᏂᏬᏂ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏓᏅᏛᏍᎬ
segments.translation: They just talk to each other in English, not Cherokee. We all speak Cherokee to each other. Also, they talk to me in Creek. ’Cause Mom was a full-blood Creek. And my late grandpa. He used to talk to me all in Creek. And then my dad, in Cherokee. That’s why I barely knew English, until I started school, that’s where I learned it. Today, the children that are growing up aren’t speaking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.text: ᏙᎯᏳ, ᎯᎮᏂ ᏥᏕᏓᏝᏃᎮ ᏍᎩ ᎯᎮᏂ ᏥᏓᏂᏱᏗ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎤᏅᏙᏗ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏥᏓᎾᏕᎳᏆᎢ ᏳᎵᏍᏙᏗᏭ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎦᏬᏂᏓ ᏥᏗᏬᏂ ᎤᏛᏁᏟᏴᏍᏗ ᏂᎨᎲᏂ ᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏍᎫ ᏔᎷᏗ ᏓᎬᏩᏟ ᎯᎢ
segments.translation: That’s true. That’s why we’re talking like this. They’re recording to use it here for the students. How Cherokee language is supposed to be, how we all speak it, without changes. There are two purposes for this.

segments.speaker: lillie-vann
segments.text: ᎨᎵᏍᎪ Ꮫ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏓᎾᏕᎳᏆ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏣᎾᏗᎰ ᏙᎮᏂ ᎠᏂᏣᎳᎩ ᏱᎦ ᎡᎵᏍᏓ ᎠᏣᎳᎩᎭ ᏯᏂᏬᏂ ᏣᎳᎩᎭ Ꮕ ᏱᏓᏂᏃᎩ ᎪᎯᏅ ᏥᎦ ᏧᏂᎳᏫᏍᏗ Ꮭ ᏱᏣᎷᏥ ᎠᏂᏣᎳᎩ ᏧᏂᎳᏫᏍᏗ ᎠᏎᏛ ᏲᏁᎦ ᏕᎧᏃᎩ ᎩᎶ Ꮧ ᏱᏥᎦᏔ ᎠᏯ ᏛᏲ ᏲᏁᎦ Ꮭ ᏱᏥᎦᏔ ᎦᏥᏲᎮᎰ
segments.translation: That’s what I think, they talk about the children going to school, learning Cherokee. If they are really Cherokees, they should be talking Cherokee. And singing in Cherokee. Nowadays, when you get to a Cherokee church, they will be singing in English there. They say, “We don’t know Cherokee.” I tell them, “I don’t know English.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏅᎾᎭ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎩᎶᏫ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎧᎵ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎠᏲᏟ ᏲᏁᎦᎭ Ꮓ ᏱᎦᏬᏂ ᏯᎨᏲᏂᏅ Ꮓ ᏯᏛᏂ ᎠᎭᏂ ᏳᎷᏥ ᏯᎨᏲᏂ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎤᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎠᎯᏗᎨ ᏯᏕᏠᎩ ᏗᎦᎵᏍᏙᏗᏍᎬ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎨᏒ ᎤᏩᏒ. ᏙᎨ ᏍᏕᎵ Ꮓ ᏍᎩ ᏗᏝ? ᎯᎮᏂ ᏲᏁᎩ ᎡᎵ ᎮᏂ Ꮩ ᏳᏩᏅᏍᏓᏂᏓ ᎧᎵ Ꮎ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎨᏒ ᎠᎯᏗᎨ Ꭸ ᏯᏕᏠᎩ ᏳᎷᏥᏌ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎦᏬᏂᏓ ᎨᎲ ᏍᏕᎵᎰ Ꭸ ᏂᎯ
segments.translation: How about what you were saying a little bit ago? If there is a full-blood Cherokee child and it’s speaking all in English. When he is taught, you could say, when he is taught to speak Cherokee, do you think he would learn to speak Cherokee easier, because he is full-blood Cherokee? If it was a white child, it might be hard on them. If it was a full-blood Cherokee, would they learn Cherokee easier? Would it come to him easier to speak Cherokee? Is that what you two think?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎾᎮᏂ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏲᏟ ᎠᏣᎳᎩᎭ ᏱᎦᏬᏂ Ꮓ ᏳᎴᏅ ᏓᏕᎳᏆᏍᎬ ᎤᏩᎨᏍᎪ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏳᏩᎨᏫ
segments.translation: Well, too, if a full-blood Cherokee child is speaking Cherokee, then they start going to school, they forget Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It won’t…

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.translation: It’s all English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It won’t…

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᎤᏩᏒᎯᏭ ᏯᎯᎵᏭ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎥᏝᏃᎮᏔᎾ ᏍᎩ ᏱᎦ
segments.translation: He could go on, himself, and be speaking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏢᎮ ᎧᎵ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎨᏒ ᏱᎬᏳᎵᏍᏕᏝᏙᏗ ᏭᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏭᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ?
segments.translation: Just because he’s full-blood, that doesn’t mean it would help him to learn Cherokee better?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏧᎾᏓᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏛᎮ ᏳᎾᏝᏃᎮᏗ ᏂᎦᏓ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏳᎾᏝᏃᎮᏗ
segments.translation: Well, if his parents speak to him, all in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᎯᏗᎨᏍᏗ ᏯᏕᏠᎩ ᏂᏗᎦᎵᏍᏙᏗᏍᎬᏅ ᎧᎵ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎨᎲ ᏳᏍᏗ
segments.translation: It would be easier for him to learn, because he is a full-blood Cherokee.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That’s the real reason, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: soldier-vann
segments.text: ᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏂᎨᎵ ᎪᎢ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎦ Ꮩ ᏢᎮᏂ ᎧᎵ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏱᎦ ᏳᏕᏂ ᏢᎮᏂ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏯᏅᏝᏃᎮᏗ ᏲᏁᎦᎭ ᎮᏂ ᎠᎾᏝᏃᎮᏗ ᏧᎾᏓᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏳᏍᏗ Ꮭ ᏯᏃᏟᎪ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎤᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ. ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᏗᏩᏛᏒ ᏦᎢᎭ ᏳᏓᎴᎩ ᎥᏮᏢᏃᎮᏛ ᏧᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ ᎮᏂ ᏧᏩᏮᎴᏅᎲ ᏧᏮᎩᎧᏅ ᏧᏩᏮᎴᏅ ᎩᎳ ᏍᏗ ᎠᏮᏕᎳᏆᎥ ᎠᏬᏟᏍᏗ ᏲᏁᎦ ᎠᏂᏬᏂᎲ. ᎫᏌᏭ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏅᏭ ᏱᎦ ᏥᏥᏬᏂᏍᎬ. ᏥᏬᏂᏍᎦ ᎨᎲ
segments.translation: That’s what I think. Because, today, when a full-blood Cherokee is born, the parents don’t talk to it in Cherokee, just English. That’s why they don’t understand Cherokee, and why they can’t learn it. Me, as I was growing up, they spoke to me in three languages. It wasn’t until I started going to school, when they took me to school, I learned how to understand them speaking English. I was just speaking Cherokee and Creek. I was a speaker.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: well, ᎬᎵᎡᎵᎦ ᎬᎵᎡᎵᎦ ᏥᏕᏓᏢᏃᎲᎳ. ᏃᎴ ᏍᎫ ᏝᎦ ᏣᎳᎩᎭ ᏥᏗᏬᏂ ᎬᎵᎡᎵᎦ
segments.translation: Well, I’m glad we all got to talk. And I’m also glad we talked all in Cherokee for a while.
